definitions.beginner: A way for one program to talk to another, like how apps send requests to an AI model.
definitions.builder: The HTTP interface to a hosted model; you send messages, tools and settings, and pay per input and output token.
definitions.research: A contract exposing model inference as a service, abstracting away weights and serving infrastructure.

terms.analogy: A restaurant's order window.
terms.example: We call the API instead of hosting our own model.

definitions.beginner: How long you wait for an AI to start or finish responding.
definitions.builder: Time to first token and total generation time; drive it down with streaming, smaller models, caching and shorter outputs.
definitions.research: Wall-clock response time, dominated by prefill (compute-bound) and decode (memory-bandwidth-bound) phases.

terms.analogy: The pause between asking and hearing the answer.
terms.example: Streaming hid the latency so users stopped complaining.

definitions.beginner: How much work an AI system can handle per second across all its users.
definitions.builder: Tokens per second across concurrent requests; batching raises throughput at some cost to per-request latency.
definitions.research: Aggregate decode rate under batching, bounded by accelerator memory bandwidth and KV-cache capacity.

terms.analogy: How many cars cross the bridge per hour, not how fast one car drives.
terms.example: Continuous batching doubled our throughput.

definitions.beginner: Showing an AI's answer word by word as it's written, instead of all at once at the end.
definitions.builder: Server-sent events delivering tokens as they decode; improves perceived speed and avoids timeouts on long outputs.
definitions.research: Incremental emission of autoregressive outputs, exposing per-token latency rather than total sequence latency.

terms.analogy: Watching someone type versus waiting for the email.
terms.example: Turning on streaming made the chat feel instant.

definitions.beginner: Reusing the work an AI already did on a repeated part of your prompt so later requests are faster and cheaper.
definitions.builder: Caching the processed prefix (system prompt, docs) server-side; repeated prefixes bill at a fraction of the price. Keep stable content first.
definitions.research: Persisting KV states for shared prefixes across requests, amortising prefill compute.

terms.analogy: Keeping the oven hot between batches of cookies.
terms.example: Prompt caching cut our bill by 70 percent.

definitions.beginner: Letting an AI use outside tools, like search, a calculator or your calendar, to get things done.
definitions.builder: Declaring functions with JSON schemas; the model emits structured calls, your code runs them and returns results. Also called function calling.
definitions.research: Augmenting a policy's action space with external APIs, interleaving generation with environment observations.

terms.analogy: Giving the assistant a phone and a calculator instead of only a pen.
terms.example: With tool use, the bot checks real flight prices.

definitions.beginner: A standard way to plug apps and data sources into AI assistants, like USB for AI.
definitions.builder: An open protocol for exposing tools, resources and prompts to any compatible AI client via MCP servers.
definitions.research: A client–server JSON-RPC protocol standardising capability discovery and invocation between models and external systems.

terms.analogy: A universal power adapter for AI.
terms.example: There's an MCP server for our database now.

definitions.beginner: An AI that can take actions on its own, using tools step by step to complete a goal, not just chat.
definitions.builder: An LLM in a loop that plans, calls tools, reads results and continues until done, with guardrails and human checkpoints.
definitions.research: A policy acting over multiple steps in an environment via tool calls, pursuing goals with partial observability.

terms.analogy: Hiring a doer, not just an adviser.
terms.example: The AI agent booked the meeting room and emailed everyone.

definitions.beginner: The repeating cycle an AI agent runs, think, act, check the result, until the job is done.
definitions.builder: The control loop that sends context to the model, executes requested tool calls, appends results and repeats until a stop condition.
definitions.research: An iterated observe–reason–act process; reliability compounds multiplicatively with the number of steps.

terms.analogy: A cook tasting and adjusting until the dish is right.
terms.example: The agent loop ran 40 steps before opening the pull request.

definitions.beginner: Coordinating several AI steps or agents so they work together on a bigger task.
definitions.builder: Code that routes work between models, tools and sub-agents (parallel fan-out, handoffs, retries) and merges results.
definitions.research: Workflow composition over model calls, from fixed DAGs to model-directed multi-agent delegation.

terms.analogy: A conductor keeping the orchestra in time.
terms.example: The orchestration layer sends research to three sub-agents at once.

definitions.beginner: Several AI agents, each with its own job, working together like a team.
definitions.builder: A lead agent delegating sub-tasks to specialised workers in parallel; helps with broad research at a higher token cost.
definitions.research: Distributed problem-solving across interacting policies, with shared or partitioned context and communication protocols.

terms.analogy: A newsroom: editor, researchers, writer.
terms.example: Our multi-agent system splits a report into twelve research threads.

definitions.beginner: AI that operates a computer like a person does, looking at the screen, clicking and typing.
definitions.builder: Agents that act through screenshots plus mouse/keyboard actions, useful where no API exists, slower than direct tool calls.
definitions.research: Vision-language policies over GUI action spaces, grounding instructions in pixel coordinates.

terms.analogy: A remote assistant driving your mouse.
terms.example: Computer use lets the agent fill in the old government portal.

definitions.beginner: Building software by describing what you want to an AI and accepting its code, often without reading it closely.
definitions.builder: Prompt-driven development where AI writes most code; great for prototypes, risky for production without review and tests.
definitions.research: Natural-language programming in which specification and verification shift from code to intent and behaviour.

terms.analogy: Directing a builder by describing the house, never touching a hammer.
terms.example: She shipped the landing page in an afternoon of vibe coding.
terms.origin: Coined by Andrej Karpathy in February 2025.

definitions.beginner: An AI that writes, runs and fixes code on its own across a whole project.
definitions.builder: An agent with file, terminal and test tools that can complete multi-file changes and open pull requests.
definitions.research: Software-engineering agents evaluated on repository-level benchmarks such as SWE-bench.

terms.analogy: A junior developer who never sleeps but needs code review.
terms.example: The coding agent fixed the bug and wrote the test.

definitions.beginner: An AI assistant built into an app that helps you as you work, suggesting text or code.
definitions.builder: Inline assistance (autocomplete, chat, edits) inside an existing tool, with a human in control.
definitions.research: Human-in-the-loop assistance optimised for acceptance rate and productivity rather than autonomous completion.

terms.analogy: A co-pilot suggests, the pilot decides.
terms.example: The copilot finished my function before I did.

definitions.beginner: Letting an AI look things up before it answers, like an open-book exam.
definitions.builder: Retrieve relevant chunks from a search index and inject them into the prompt to ground the answer in your own data.
definitions.research: Conditioning generation on retrieved documents p(y | x, z) to reduce hallucination and update knowledge without retraining.

terms.analogy: An open-book exam instead of answering from memory.
terms.example: We added RAG so the support bot cites our actual docs.

definitions.beginner: A database that finds things by meaning rather than exact words.
definitions.builder: Stores embeddings and runs approximate nearest-neighbour search; the retrieval engine behind most RAG systems.
definitions.research: An index (HNSW, IVF-PQ) supporting sublinear approximate k-NN queries in high-dimensional vector spaces.

terms.analogy: A librarian who shelves books by topic, not alphabet.
terms.example: Every help article lives in the vector database.

definitions.beginner: Search that understands what you mean, not just the exact words you typed.
definitions.builder: Embedding the query and documents and ranking by vector similarity, often blended with keyword search (hybrid).
definitions.research: Dense retrieval in a learned representation space, complementing sparse lexical methods like BM25.

terms.analogy: Asking for "something cosy to read" and getting good books.
terms.example: Semantic search found the refund policy when I typed "money back".

definitions.beginner: Cutting long documents into smaller pieces so an AI search can find the right part.
definitions.builder: Splitting documents into retrievable units (by tokens, headings or semantics); chunk size strongly affects RAG quality.
definitions.research: Segmentation of corpora into retrieval units trading off context completeness against retrieval precision.

terms.analogy: Cutting a book into index cards.
terms.example: Better chunking fixed answers that mixed up two products.

definitions.beginner: A second, smarter pass that reorders search results so the best ones come first.
definitions.builder: Scoring the top-k retrieved chunks with a cross-encoder or LLM and keeping only the most relevant before generation.
definitions.research: Two-stage retrieval where an expensive joint query–document model refines a cheap first-stage candidate set.

terms.analogy: A shortlist interview after the CV screen.
terms.example: Adding reranking stopped irrelevant passages reaching the prompt.

definitions.beginner: Tests that check how well an AI system does the job you actually need it for.
definitions.builder: Task-specific test sets plus graders (code, rubric or LLM-as-judge) run on every prompt or model change, like unit tests for AI.
definitions.research: Measurement protocols estimating model capability or behaviour with attention to validity, variance and contamination.

terms.analogy: A driving test for your chatbot.
terms.example: Our evals caught the regression before launch.

definitions.beginner: Using one AI to grade another AI's answers.
definitions.builder: Scoring outputs with a model against a rubric; scalable, but validate against human labels and watch for position and length bias.
definitions.research: Automatic evaluation via model-based preference or rubric scoring, with known self-preference and verbosity biases.

terms.analogy: A teaching assistant marking papers with the professor's rubric.
terms.example: LLM-as-judge agreed with our reviewers 90% of the time.

definitions.beginner: A test that checks whether AI can fix real bugs from open-source GitHub projects.
definitions.builder: Benchmark of real GitHub issues where the model must produce a patch that passes the repo's tests; the go-to coding-agent metric.
definitions.research: Repository-level program repair evaluated by execution of held-out tests; Verified subset filters ambiguous tasks.

terms.analogy: A real job interview instead of a quiz.
terms.example: The new model scored a record on SWE-bench.

definitions.beginner: When AI models all score near 100% on a test, so it stops telling them apart.
definitions.builder: A benchmark maxed out (or contaminated) loses signal; the field moves on to harder evals.
definitions.research: Ceiling effects where residual error is dominated by label noise, eliminating discriminative power.

terms.analogy: A ruler that's too short to measure the tall kids.
terms.example: Benchmark saturation forced everyone to build harder tests.

definitions.beginner: A cheap way to customise a big model by training a tiny add-on instead of the whole thing.
definitions.builder: Freeze the base weights and train small low-rank adapter matrices; adapters are megabytes and swappable per customer.
definitions.research: Parameterising weight updates as ΔW = BA with rank r ≪ d, drastically reducing trainable parameters.

terms.analogy: A clip-on lens instead of a new camera.
terms.example: Each customer gets their own LoRA adapter.

definitions.beginner: Training a small, cheap model to copy a big, smart one.
definitions.builder: Train a student on a teacher model's outputs or probabilities; how fast "mini" models get surprisingly good.
definitions.research: Matching the student's predictive distribution to the teacher's soft targets, transferring dark knowledge.

terms.analogy: A master chef's apprentice learning by watching.
terms.example: The mini model is a distillation of the big one.

definitions.beginner: Shrinking a model by storing its numbers with less precision, so it runs faster on smaller hardware.
definitions.builder: Converting weights (and sometimes activations) to 8- or 4-bit; big memory and speed wins for small quality loss.
definitions.research: Mapping parameters to low-bit discrete grids (GPTQ, AWQ) while minimising reconstruction error of layer outputs.

terms.analogy: Saving a photo as a smaller JPEG.
terms.example: Quantization lets the model run on a laptop.

definitions.beginner: AI that runs directly on your phone or laptop instead of in the cloud.
definitions.builder: Small, quantised models on NPUs; private and offline with no per-call cost, but limited capability.
definitions.research: Inference under tight memory, power and thermal budgets using compression and hardware-specific kernels.

terms.analogy: A pocket calculator versus calling the bank.
terms.example: Edge AI summarises your messages without uploading them.

definitions.beginner: A compact language model that is cheaper and faster, good enough for focused tasks.
definitions.builder: Models of roughly 1–10B parameters for routing, extraction and on-device use; often distilled from larger ones.
definitions.research: Parameter-efficient models trading generality for latency and cost, benefiting from over-training and distillation.

terms.analogy: A scooter for short trips instead of a truck.
terms.example: An SLM classifies tickets before the big model sees them.

definitions.beginner: An AI that "thinks" privately before answering, which makes it much better at maths, code and planning.
definitions.builder: Models trained with RL to produce long internal reasoning before the answer; tune the effort or thinking budget per task.
definitions.research: Policies trained via RL on verifiable rewards to exploit test-time compute through extended chains of thought.

terms.analogy: A student allowed scratch paper.
terms.example: Use the reasoning model for the tax calculations.

definitions.beginner: Letting an AI spend more thinking time on a hard question to get a better answer.
definitions.builder: Spending more inference tokens (longer reasoning, multiple samples, verification) to raise accuracy; a new scaling axis.
definitions.research: Scaling performance with inference FLOPs via sequential reasoning or parallel sampling, complementing pre-training scale.

terms.analogy: Giving someone an hour for the puzzle instead of a minute.
terms.example: Test-time compute doubled its score on the olympiad problems.

definitions.beginner: Training an AI on problems where answers can be checked automatically, like maths or passing code tests.
definitions.builder: RL with programmatic graders (unit tests, exact answers) instead of human ratings; the recipe behind reasoning models.
definitions.research: Policy optimisation with binary or graded rewards from deterministic verifiers, enabling scalable reasoning RL.

terms.analogy: Practising with an answer key instead of a human tutor.
terms.example: RLVR on maths problems taught it to check its own work.

definitions.beginner: A training method where an AI tries a problem several times and learns from which attempts beat its own average.
definitions.builder: PPO variant without a critic; advantages come from comparing rewards within a group of samples for the same prompt.
definitions.research: Policy gradient with group-normalised advantages (r − mean)/std over k samples, removing the value network.

terms.analogy: Grading your attempts on a curve against each other.
terms.example: DeepSeek used GRPO to train its reasoning model cheaply.

definitions.beginner: A popular, careful way to train AI with rewards that avoids changing it too much at once.
definitions.builder: The classic RL algorithm behind early RLHF; clipped updates and a learned value model keep training stable.
definitions.research: Policy-gradient method maximising a clipped surrogate objective, bounding the probability ratio between successive policies.

terms.analogy: Adjusting a recipe a pinch at a time.
terms.example: PPO powered the original ChatGPT fine-tune.

definitions.beginner: Combining keyword search with meaning-based search to get the best of both.
definitions.builder: Fusing BM25 and vector results (e.g. reciprocal rank fusion); catches exact IDs and paraphrases alike.
definitions.research: Ensemble of sparse and dense retrievers exploiting complementary failure modes.

terms.analogy: Using both the index and a librarian's hunch.
terms.example: Hybrid search finally found error code E-1042.

definitions.beginner: How an AI remembers things about you or a task between conversations.
definitions.builder: Persisting facts, preferences and notes outside the context window (files, databases) and pulling them back in when relevant.
definitions.research: External read/write stores that extend an agent's effective state beyond its fixed context length.

terms.analogy: A notebook the assistant keeps between meetings.
terms.example: Agent memory means I don't re-explain my project every day.

definitions.beginner: A setup where a person checks or approves an AI's work at key moments.
definitions.builder: Approval gates on risky actions (payments, deletes, sends) inside agent workflows.
definitions.research: Mixed-initiative systems where human oversight bounds the consequences of policy errors.

terms.analogy: A pilot who can always take the controls.
terms.example: Refunds over $100 stay human-in-the-loop.

definitions.beginner: Computer systems that do things we'd normally call smart, like writing, seeing or deciding.
definitions.builder: The broad field of building software that performs tasks requiring perception, language, reasoning or planning.
definitions.research: The study of agents that perceive their environment and act to maximise some objective, spanning search, learning and inference.

terms.analogy: An umbrella word, like "transport" covers bikes and planes.
terms.example: Every app now claims to have AI inside.
terms.origin: Coined by John McCarthy for the 1956 Dartmouth workshop.

definitions.beginner: Teaching computers by showing them lots of examples instead of writing every rule by hand.
definitions.builder: Fitting a model's parameters to data so it generalises to new inputs, rather than hand-coding logic.
definitions.research: Algorithms that improve performance on a task with experience, typically by minimising an empirical loss over a hypothesis class.

terms.analogy: Learning to cook by tasting many dishes rather than memorising a rulebook.
terms.example: The spam filter uses machine learning to spot new scams.

definitions.beginner: The trained "brain" file that an AI app runs to produce answers.
definitions.builder: A learned function, its architecture plus trained weights, that maps inputs to outputs and is served behind an API.
definitions.research: A parameterised function f(x; θ) whose parameters θ were estimated from data to approximate a target distribution or mapping.

terms.analogy: A recipe the computer wrote for itself after tasting millions of meals.
terms.example: They swapped in a smaller model to cut costs.

definitions.beginner: A step-by-step set of instructions a computer follows to solve a problem.
definitions.builder: A finite, well-defined procedure. In ML, the training procedure is the algorithm and the trained model is its output.
definitions.research: An effective procedure computing a function; in learning theory, the map from a training sample to a hypothesis.

terms.analogy: A recipe: do this, then this, until done.
terms.example: The feed is ranked by an algorithm nobody fully understands.

definitions.beginner: Software made of layers of tiny math units, loosely inspired by brain cells, that learns patterns from data.
definitions.builder: Stacked layers of weighted sums and nonlinearities trained with gradient descent; the backbone of modern AI.
definitions.research: A composition of affine maps and elementwise nonlinearities, a universal function approximator optimised via backpropagation.

terms.analogy: A huge team passing notes, each adjusting how loudly they listen to their neighbours.
terms.example: A neural network learned to read handwriting from scanned cheques.

definitions.beginner: Machine learning with very big neural networks that have many layers.
definitions.builder: Training deep neural networks end-to-end on large datasets, usually on GPUs; behind vision, speech and LLMs.
definitions.research: Representation learning with deep, differentiable architectures where hierarchical features emerge from gradient-based optimisation.

terms.analogy: Learning to recognise a face by first spotting edges, then eyes, then whole faces.
terms.example: Deep learning took image recognition from a research toy to your phone camera.
terms.origin: Popularised after AlexNet won ImageNet in 2012.

definitions.beginner: The expensive phase where a model learns by practising on huge amounts of data.
definitions.builder: Running optimisation over a dataset to update model weights; costly, done once (or periodically), unlike inference.
definitions.research: Minimising expected loss over the data distribution via stochastic gradient methods, typically for many steps across accelerators.

terms.analogy: Years of school, versus inference which is sitting the exam.
terms.example: Training the model took three months on thousands of GPUs.

definitions.beginner: When a finished model is used to answer you, as opposed to when it was learning.
definitions.builder: Running a trained model forward to produce outputs; where latency, cost per token and serving infrastructure matter.
definitions.research: Evaluating the learned function (and decoding procedure) on new inputs with frozen parameters.

terms.analogy: Sitting the exam after all the studying is done.
terms.example: Inference costs dropped tenfold this year.

definitions.beginner: The big pile of examples, like text, images or clicks, that a model learns from.
definitions.builder: A curated collection of examples split into train / validation / test sets; its quality caps model quality.
definitions.research: A finite sample assumed drawn from the target distribution; biases and contamination in it propagate to the model.

terms.analogy: The textbook a student learns from. A bad textbook makes a bad student.
terms.example: They cleaned the training data and the model got noticeably better.

definitions.beginner: One of the billions of adjustable numbers inside a model that store what it learned.
definitions.builder: A trainable weight or bias. Parameter count (e.g. 70B) is a rough proxy for size, memory and cost.
definitions.research: An element of θ, the vector optimised during training; count scales compute and memory roughly linearly.

terms.analogy: Billions of tiny dials, each tuned slightly during training.
terms.example: The open model has 70 billion parameters.

definitions.beginner: The saved numbers that make up a trained model, basically the model itself as a file.
definitions.builder: The tensor values learned in training; "releasing the weights" means anyone can download and run the model.
definitions.research: Learned parameters of the network's linear maps, usually stored in bf16/fp8; their distribution informs quantisation strategies.

terms.analogy: The model's memory written to disk.
terms.example: The lab published the model weights under a permissive licence.

definitions.beginner: How a model improves: it checks which way makes it less wrong, then takes a small step that way, millions of times.
definitions.builder: The optimisation loop: compute the loss gradient, nudge weights against it by the learning rate, repeat (usually Adam-style variants).
definitions.research: Iterative first-order optimisation θ ← θ − η∇L(θ); stochastic mini-batch variants with momentum dominate deep learning.

terms.analogy: Walking downhill in fog by always stepping where the ground slopes down.
terms.example: Gradient descent slowly pushed the loss toward zero.

definitions.beginner: A score of how wrong the model is. Training tries to make it as small as possible.
definitions.builder: The objective being minimised; cross-entropy for next-token prediction, plus extras like KL penalties in RL fine-tuning.
definitions.research: A function L(ŷ, y) measuring discrepancy between prediction and target; its expectation is the risk minimised in training.

terms.analogy: The red ink on a marked test paper.
terms.example: The loss function stopped dropping after day four.

definitions.beginner: How big a step the model takes each time it adjusts itself. Too big and it overshoots, too small and it barely moves.
definitions.builder: The step-size hyperparameter, usually with warmup and cosine decay; the first knob to tune when training diverges.
definitions.research: Scalar η scaling each update; schedules and per-parameter adaptation (Adam) critically shape convergence and generalisation.

terms.analogy: Stride length when walking downhill in the dark.
terms.example: We halved the learning rate and the training run stopped exploding.

definitions.beginner: One full pass through all the training data.
definitions.builder: A complete pass over the training set; LLM pre-training often runs ~1 epoch, while fine-tunes run a few.
definitions.research: One traversal of the empirical dataset; multi-epoch training on finite data raises memorisation and overfitting risk.

terms.analogy: Reading the whole textbook once, cover to cover.
terms.example: The fine-tune ran for three epochs.

definitions.beginner: When a model memorises its practice examples so well it does badly on anything new.
definitions.builder: Training loss keeps falling while validation loss rises; fix with more data, regularisation or early stopping.
definitions.research: High variance: the hypothesis fits sample noise, widening the generalisation gap between empirical and true risk.

terms.analogy: A student who memorised last year's answers but can't handle a new question.
terms.example: The validation curve showed clear overfitting after epoch two.

definitions.beginner: A model's ability to handle new situations it never saw during training.
definitions.builder: Performance on held-out data, the thing you actually care about; measured on a test set the model never trained on.
definitions.research: The gap between empirical and population risk; bounded classically by capacity, empirically puzzling for overparameterised nets.

terms.analogy: Understanding the rules, not just memorising past games.
terms.example: Good generalization means it works on your messy real-world data too.

definitions.beginner: The first, giant stage where a model reads a huge chunk of the internet and learns how language works.
definitions.builder: Self-supervised next-token training on trillions of tokens, producing a base model that later post-training shapes into an assistant.
definitions.research: Large-scale self-supervised learning of p(x) on broad corpora, yielding transferable representations; dominates total compute.

terms.analogy: Reading the entire library before ever being asked a question.
terms.example: Pre-training alone cost more than the whole company's first round.

definitions.beginner: The later training that turns a raw text-predictor into a helpful, safe assistant.
definitions.builder: Everything after pre-training: instruction tuning, RLHF/RLAIF, safety training and tool-use tuning that shape behaviour.
definitions.research: Fine-tuning and RL stages that reshape the pre-trained distribution toward preferred policies under KL constraints.

terms.analogy: Finishing school after a lifetime of reading.
terms.example: Most of the model's personality comes from post-training.

definitions.beginner: A model straight out of pre-training. It continues text well but isn't yet good at following instructions.
definitions.builder: The raw pre-trained checkpoint, great for fine-tuning and completion, awkward as a chatbot without instruction tuning.
definitions.research: The pre-trained density model prior to any alignment, often better calibrated than post-trained variants.

terms.analogy: A brilliant mimic who hasn't been taught manners.
terms.example: The base model just kept writing more questions instead of answering.

definitions.beginner: Extra training on a smaller, specific set of examples so a general model gets good at one job.
definitions.builder: Continuing training on task data to change behaviour or style. Great for format and tone, poor for injecting fresh facts.
definitions.research: Further optimisation of pre-trained parameters on a narrower distribution, fully or via parameter-efficient methods like LoRA.

terms.analogy: A trained chef doing a month at a sushi bar.
terms.example: We tried fine-tuning on our support tickets to match our tone.

definitions.beginner: Training examples created by AI instead of collected from people.
definitions.builder: Model-generated training data, filtered and verified, used to cover gaps, reasoning traces or rare cases cheaply.
definitions.research: Samples from generative models used as training signal; quality filtering prevents distribution collapse ("model collapse").

terms.analogy: Practice exams written by a teacher instead of past papers.
terms.example: Half the fine-tuning set was synthetic data checked by a verifier.

definitions.beginner: When test questions accidentally end up in the training data, so the model "cheats" without meaning to.
definitions.builder: Benchmark items leaking into pre-training corpora, inflating scores; mitigated by held-out, fresh or private eval sets.
definitions.research: Overlap between evaluation and training distributions that invalidates the i.i.d. held-out assumption behind reported metrics.

terms.analogy: Seeing the exam paper the night before.
terms.example: The suspicious jump in scores turned out to be data contamination.

definitions.beginner: A small chunk of text, often part of a word, that language models read and write. Roughly ¾ of a word.
definitions.builder: The unit models process and bill by; ~4 characters of English. Context limits, pricing and speed are all in tokens.
definitions.research: A discrete symbol from the tokenizer's vocabulary; sequences of token ids are the model's actual input and output space.

terms.analogy: Lego bricks of language.
terms.example: That long prompt used 12,000 tokens.

definitions.beginner: The tool that chops text into tokens before the model sees it.
definitions.builder: Maps text to token ids (usually BPE); explains odd behaviour like miscounting letters, and why other languages cost more.
definitions.research: A learned subword segmentation (BPE, unigram) balancing vocabulary size against sequence length and cross-lingual coverage.

terms.analogy: A butcher deciding where to cut the sentence.
terms.example: The tokenizer splits "strawberry" into chunks, which is why it miscounts the r's.

definitions.beginner: A common way of splitting text into tokens by merging the most frequent letter pairs.
definitions.builder: The subword tokenization algorithm behind most LLM vocabularies; frequent strings become single tokens.
definitions.research: Greedy iterative merging of the most frequent adjacent symbol pairs from bytes up to a target vocabulary size.

terms.analogy: Inventing abbreviations for the phrases you write most.
terms.example: Byte-level BPE means the model never meets an unknown character.
terms.origin: Adapted for neural machine translation by Sennrich et al., 2016.

definitions.beginner: A list of numbers that captures what something means, so similar things end up close together.
definitions.builder: A dense vector from an embedding model; compare with cosine similarity for search, clustering and RAG retrieval.
definitions.research: A learned map into ℝᵈ where geometric relations (distance, direction) encode semantic relations between inputs.

terms.analogy: GPS coordinates for meaning.
terms.example: We store an embedding for every help article.

definitions.beginner: The design behind ChatGPT, Claude and most modern AI. It looks at all the words at once to understand context.
definitions.builder: The architecture of stacked attention + MLP blocks that powers LLMs; parallelises well on GPUs, which is why it scaled.
definitions.research: A sequence model built from multi-head self-attention and position-wise feed-forward layers with residual connections and normalisation.

terms.analogy: A meeting where everyone can hear everyone, instead of a game of telephone.
terms.example: The "T" in GPT stands for transformer.
terms.origin: "Attention Is All You Need", Vaswani et al., Google, 2017.

definitions.beginner: How a model decides which earlier words matter most for the word it's working on now.
definitions.builder: The transformer mechanism that mixes information across tokens; cost grows with the square of the context length.
definitions.research: softmax(QKᵀ/√d)V, a content-based weighted average letting each position aggregate information from all others.

terms.analogy: Highlighting the parts of a page relevant to your question.
terms.example: Attention lets "it" link back to "the cat" three sentences earlier.

definitions.beginner: An AI trained on huge amounts of text that can write, summarise, answer and chat. Claude and ChatGPT are LLMs.
definitions.builder: A large transformer trained to predict the next token, then post-trained to follow instructions and use tools.
definitions.research: An autoregressive model of p(xₜ | x<t) with billions of parameters, trained on web-scale corpora; capabilities scale with compute.

terms.analogy: Autocomplete that read the whole library.
terms.example: Our app calls an LLM to draft replies.

definitions.beginner: A big general-purpose AI model that many different apps are built on top of.
definitions.builder: A broadly pre-trained model adapted to many downstream tasks via prompting or fine-tuning; a key category in AI regulation.
definitions.research: A model trained on broad data at scale that is adaptable to a wide range of tasks, a term from Stanford's CRFM.

terms.analogy: A building's foundation: many different houses go on top.
terms.example: Dozens of startups are wrappers around the same foundation model.

definitions.beginner: AI that creates new things, like text, images, music or code, instead of just sorting or predicting.
definitions.builder: Models that sample new content from a learned distribution: LLMs, diffusion image models, audio and video generators.
definitions.research: Models of p(x) (or p(x|c)) from which novel samples are drawn: autoregressive, diffusion, flow-based or GAN families.

terms.analogy: A camera captures; generative AI paints.
terms.example: Generative AI wrote the first draft of the ad.

definitions.beginner: Able to handle more than one kind of input or output, like text, images and audio together.
definitions.builder: Models that accept or produce multiple modalities; e.g. paste a screenshot and ask about it.
definitions.research: Joint modelling across modalities via shared token spaces or cross-attention, enabling grounding of language in perception.

terms.analogy: A person who can read, look and listen at the same time.
terms.example: The multimodal model read the chart in my screenshot.

definitions.beginner: How much text a model can keep in mind at once, its working memory, measured in tokens.
definitions.builder: The max tokens (prompt + output) per request; 1M-token windows fit whole codebases, but cost and latency grow with length.
definitions.research: The maximum sequence length the model attends over, bounded by positional encoding range and attention's memory cost.

terms.analogy: The size of the desk you can spread papers on.
terms.example: The whole contract fits in the context window.

definitions.beginner: The date a model's training data ends. It doesn't know about anything after that unless you tell it.
definitions.builder: The last date covered by training data; supply fresher facts via search tools or RAG.
definitions.research: The temporal boundary of the pre-training corpus; post-cutoff knowledge must come from retrieval or context.

terms.analogy: A letter from someone who has been at sea since last spring.
terms.example: Its knowledge cutoff is last year, so it missed the election.

definitions.beginner: A standard test used to compare AI models, like an exam everyone sits.
definitions.builder: A fixed dataset and metric (e.g. SWE-bench, MMLU) for comparing models; useful but gameable and prone to saturation.
definitions.research: A standardised evaluation protocol; validity threatened by contamination, saturation and Goodhart effects.

terms.analogy: A standardised test: useful to compare, but students can learn to the test.
terms.example: The new model tops every benchmark, but how does it feel to use?

definitions.beginner: A model whose trained files are released so anyone can download and run it themselves.
definitions.builder: Downloadable weights you can self-host and fine-tune. Not always "open source": training data and code may stay closed.
definitions.research: Public release of trained parameters (often under use restrictions), enabling replication of inference but not of training.

terms.analogy: Getting the finished cake recipe, but not the farm that grew the ingredients.
terms.example: Llama made open weights mainstream.

definitions.beginner: An AI model that is freely shared so anyone can use, study and change it.
definitions.builder: Ideally weights + code + data under an OSI-style licence; in practice many "open" models share weights only.
definitions.research: Release meeting the Open Source AI Definition: weights, training code and sufficient data information to reproduce.

terms.analogy: A community garden instead of a private farm.
terms.example: The startup built on an open-source model to avoid API fees.

definitions.beginner: A model you can only use through the company's app or API. You can't download it.
definitions.builder: Proprietary model served via API only; you get managed scaling and frontier quality, trading off control and data residency.
definitions.research: A model whose parameters are withheld; external evaluation is limited to black-box query access.

terms.analogy: Eating at the restaurant versus getting the recipe.
terms.example: Most frontier labs ship a closed model behind an API.

definitions.beginner: The finding that AI models get predictably better as you add more data, compute and size.
definitions.builder: Empirical power laws predicting loss from parameters, data and compute; used to plan training runs before spending millions.
definitions.research: L(N, D) ≈ E + A/N^α + B/D^β; smooth power-law relations between loss and scale across many orders of magnitude.

terms.analogy: A recipe that says doubling the oven size makes the cake better by a predictable amount.
terms.example: Scaling laws told them exactly how big the next model should be.
terms.origin: Kaplan et al. (OpenAI) 2020; refined by Hoffmann et al. (Chinchilla) 2022.

definitions.beginner: The rule of thumb that a model should be trained on about 20 words of data for every one of its parameters.
definitions.builder: Compute-optimal balance of ~20 tokens per parameter; modern models deliberately "over-train" smaller models for cheaper inference.
definitions.research: The allocation minimising loss for fixed FLOPs C ≈ 6ND, finding N and D should scale roughly equally with compute.

terms.analogy: Matching the size of the student to the size of the library.
terms.example: The model was trained far past Chinchilla-optimal to make it cheap to serve.

definitions.beginner: Skills that seem to suddenly appear once a model gets big enough.
definitions.builder: Capabilities absent in small models that show up at scale. Some apparent jumps are artifacts of all-or-nothing metrics.
definitions.research: Discontinuous task-metric gains with scale; debated, since continuous metrics often reveal smooth underlying improvement.

terms.analogy: Water suddenly boiling after degrees of quiet warming.
terms.example: Emergent abilities make it hard to predict what the next model can do.
terms.origin: Wei et al., 2022; challenged by Schaeffer et al., 2023.

definitions.beginner: The raw computer processing power used to train and run AI, mostly from specialised chips.
definitions.builder: Accelerator capacity (GPU/TPU hours, FLOPs); the main cost driver and bottleneck for labs and AI products.
definitions.research: Total floating-point operations; training compute C ≈ 6 × parameters × tokens for dense transformers.

terms.analogy: The electricity and engines of the AI economy.
terms.example: The lab signed a ten-billion-dollar compute deal.

definitions.beginner: A chip that does thousands of calculations at once. The workhorse for training and running AI.
definitions.builder: Massively parallel accelerators (e.g. NVIDIA H100/B200) whose memory and interconnect bound model size and speed.
definitions.research: SIMT processors with high-bandwidth memory and tensor cores optimised for dense matrix multiplication.

terms.analogy: A thousand cashiers instead of one very fast one.
terms.example: The startup's biggest expense is GPU rental.

definitions.beginner: Google's own AI chip, built specifically for neural network math.
definitions.builder: Google's ASIC accelerators, rented via Google Cloud, linked in large pods for training and serving.
definitions.research: Systolic-array matrix units with high-bandwidth interconnect, optimised for bf16 tensor operations at pod scale.

terms.analogy: A custom race car versus a fast sports car.
terms.example: The model was trained on TPU pods.

definitions.beginner: A huge building full of computers where AI models are trained and run.
definitions.builder: Facilities housing accelerator clusters; power, cooling and interconnect now limit AI expansion as much as chips.
definitions.research: Warehouse-scale computers whose network topology and power envelope shape feasible training-run sizes.

terms.analogy: The factory floor of the AI economy.
terms.example: The new data center will draw as much power as a city.

definitions.beginner: A memory trick that lets a model avoid re-reading the whole conversation for every new word.
definitions.builder: Stored key/value tensors for past tokens; makes generation fast but eats GPU memory that grows with context length.
definitions.research: Cached attention keys and values enabling O(n) per-step decoding at O(n·layers·d) memory per sequence.

terms.analogy: Keeping notes on what you've read instead of re-reading the book every page.
terms.example: Long chats blow up the KV cache.

definitions.beginner: A faster way to compute attention that uses chip memory more cleverly.
definitions.builder: An IO-aware attention kernel that tiles the computation in fast SRAM; standard in training and serving stacks.
definitions.research: Exact attention via tiling and online softmax to avoid materialising the n×n matrix in HBM.

terms.analogy: Cooking in small batches on the counter instead of running to the fridge for every ingredient.
terms.example: FlashAttention made long-context training affordable.

definitions.beginner: A way of storing an AI's short-term memory in small pages so many users can share a GPU efficiently.
definitions.builder: KV-cache memory managed like OS virtual-memory pages (vLLM); cuts fragmentation and raises serving throughput.
definitions.research: Non-contiguous block allocation of KV caches with indirection tables, enabling sharing and near-zero waste.

terms.analogy: Hotel rooms assigned as guests arrive, instead of reserving whole floors.
terms.example: Switching to PagedAttention let us serve 3x more users.

definitions.beginner: Mixing many users' requests together on the fly so the chips are never idle.
definitions.builder: Iteration-level scheduling that adds and removes sequences each decode step instead of waiting for whole batches.
definitions.research: Dynamic batch composition at token granularity, maximising accelerator utilisation under variable-length requests.

terms.analogy: A bus that lets people on and off at every stop.
terms.example: Continuous batching cut our GPU bill in half.

definitions.beginner: Speeding up an AI by letting a small model guess ahead and the big model check the guesses.
definitions.builder: A draft model proposes several tokens; the target verifies them in one pass. Same output distribution, lower latency.
definitions.research: Rejection-sampling-based verification of draft tokens that preserves the target distribution exactly.

terms.analogy: An intern drafts, the expert just approves.
terms.example: Speculative decoding made responses twice as fast.

definitions.beginner: Splitting each layer of a giant model across several chips so they share the work.
definitions.builder: Sharding individual matrix multiplies across GPUs in a node; needs very fast interconnect such as NVLink.
definitions.research: Intra-layer model parallelism partitioning weight matrices, with all-reduce communication per layer.

terms.analogy: Several chefs working on the same dish at once.
terms.example: Tensor parallelism spreads the model over eight GPUs.

definitions.beginner: Giving different chips different layers of a model, like stations on an assembly line.
definitions.builder: Partitioning layers across devices and streaming micro-batches through; reduces memory per device, adds pipeline bubbles.
definitions.research: Inter-layer parallelism with micro-batch scheduling (GPipe, 1F1B) trading bubble overhead for memory.

terms.analogy: A car factory assembly line.
terms.example: Pipeline parallelism let the model span two nodes.

definitions.beginner: A training method that spreads a model's memory across many chips so bigger models fit.
definitions.builder: Shards parameters, gradients and optimiser state across data-parallel workers, gathering them just in time per layer.
definitions.research: ZeRO-3-style sharding of training state, reducing per-device memory at the cost of extra communication.

terms.analogy: Everyone carries part of the luggage.
terms.example: FSDP let us train a 30B model on our cluster.

definitions.beginner: A very compact number format that makes AI chips run faster with little loss in quality.
definitions.builder: 8-bit floating point for training and inference on recent GPUs; nearly 2x throughput over bf16 with careful scaling.
definitions.research: E4M3/E5M2 formats with per-tensor or per-block scaling to keep activations and gradients in representable range.

terms.analogy: Rounding prices to the nearest dollar to add up faster.
terms.example: The run used FP8 for most matrix multiplies.

definitions.beginner: A model built from many specialist parts, where only a few switch on for each word, saving effort.
definitions.builder: MoE layers route each token to a few expert FFNs; huge total parameters with modest per-token compute, but heavy memory.
definitions.research: Sparse conditional computation with a learned router selecting top-k experts per token, with load-balancing losses.

terms.analogy: A hospital where each patient sees only the relevant specialists.
terms.example: It's a mixture of experts with 600B parameters but only 37B active.

definitions.beginner: The method that works out how much each part of a neural network contributed to a mistake, so it can be adjusted.
definitions.builder: Reverse-mode autodiff computing gradients of the loss for every weight; frameworks like PyTorch do it automatically.
definitions.research: Efficient application of the chain rule through the computational graph, costing roughly 2x the forward pass.

terms.analogy: Tracing back through a relay race to see who dropped the baton.
terms.example: Backpropagation computes the gradient for all 70 billion weights.

definitions.beginner: A math step that turns raw scores into probabilities that add up to 100%.
definitions.builder: Normalises logits into a probability distribution; used for next-token prediction and inside attention.
definitions.research: σ(z)ᵢ = e^{zᵢ} / Σⱼ e^{zⱼ}, a smooth argmax whose temperature controls entropy.

terms.analogy: Turning vote counts into vote shares.
terms.example: The final softmax gives each possible next token a probability.

definitions.beginner: The standard score for how surprised a model is by the right answer. Lower is better.
definitions.builder: The next-token training loss; its exponential is perplexity.
definitions.research: H(p, q) = −Σ p log q; minimising it equals maximum likelihood and minimising KL to the data distribution.

terms.analogy: How shocked you are by the plot twist.
terms.example: Cross-entropy kept falling as we added data.

definitions.beginner: A measure of how confused a language model is by some text. Lower means it predicts better.
definitions.builder: exp(cross-entropy); handy for comparing pre-training runs, weakly tied to how useful a chatbot feels.
definitions.research: The exponentiated average negative log-likelihood, the effective branching factor of the model's predictions.

terms.analogy: How many words it's torn between at each step.
terms.example: Perplexity dropped after we cleaned the data.

definitions.beginner: A measure of how different two probability patterns are.
definitions.builder: Used as a leash in RLHF so the tuned model doesn't drift too far from the original.
definitions.research: D_KL(P‖Q) = Σ P log(P/Q); asymmetric, non-negative, zero iff distributions match.

terms.analogy: How surprised you'd be using one map to navigate the other's city.
terms.example: The KL divergence penalty stopped the model from going off the rails.

definitions.beginner: Extra information that tells a transformer the order of words, since it otherwise sees them all at once.
definitions.builder: Position signals added to token representations; RoPE is the modern default and limits how far context can stretch.
definitions.research: Injecting order into permutation-invariant attention via absolute, relative or rotary (RoPE) schemes.

terms.analogy: Page numbers on loose sheets.
terms.example: A new positional encoding let the model read million-token inputs.

definitions.beginner: A clever way of encoding word positions by rotating numbers, used in most modern models.
definitions.builder: Rotates query/key vectors by position-dependent angles; context extension tricks (YaRN, NTK scaling) modify its frequencies.
definitions.research: Multiplicative rotation in 2D subspaces making attention scores depend on relative offset m−n.

terms.analogy: Clock hands: the angle between them tells the distance.
terms.example: They stretched RoPE to reach a longer context window.

definitions.beginner: The surprising pattern where making a model bigger first hurts, then helps again.
definitions.builder: Test error peaks near the interpolation threshold, then falls with more parameters; part of why huge models generalise.
definitions.research: Non-monotonic risk curve in model size or epochs, contradicting the classical U-shaped bias–variance picture.

terms.analogy: It gets worse before it gets better.
terms.example: Double descent explains why bigger wasn't always worse.

definitions.beginner: When a model suddenly "gets it" long after it seemed to have just memorised the training examples.
definitions.builder: Delayed generalisation after near-zero training loss, observed on small algorithmic tasks with weight decay.
definitions.research: A phase transition from memorising to generalising circuits, interpretable via mechanistic analysis.

terms.analogy: The moment long division finally clicks.
terms.example: Training kept going and the model hit grokking at step 40,000.

definitions.beginner: An image AI that starts with random noise and gradually cleans it up into a picture.
definitions.builder: The generator behind most image and video models; denoises over many steps, guided by a text prompt.
definitions.research: Learning to reverse a Gaussian noising process via score matching, sampling by iterative denoising.

terms.analogy: A sculptor removing marble until a statue appears.
terms.example: A diffusion model made the album cover.

definitions.beginner: A newer, faster way to train image and video generators by learning smooth paths from noise to pictures.
definitions.builder: Trains a velocity field along straight paths from noise to data; fewer sampling steps than classic diffusion.
definitions.research: Regressing a time-dependent vector field generating a probability path between prior and data (continuous normalising flows).

terms.analogy: Drawing the straightest road from scribble to picture.
terms.example: The video model switched to flow matching.

definitions.beginner: An AI that understands both pictures and text, so you can ask questions about an image.
definitions.builder: An LLM with a vision encoder; reads screenshots, charts, documents and photos.
definitions.research: Multimodal models aligning visual encoders with language decoders via projection or cross-attention.

terms.analogy: A reader who can also look at the illustrations.
terms.example: The VLM read the receipt and filled in the expense form.

definitions.beginner: Using AI to copy someone's voice from a short recording.
definitions.builder: Few-shot speech synthesis conditioned on a speaker sample; useful for dubbing, abused for scams. Consent and watermarks matter.
definitions.research: Speaker-conditioned TTS generalising from seconds of reference audio via learned speaker embeddings.

terms.analogy: A vocal photocopier.
terms.example: Voice cloning scams target grandparents.

definitions.beginner: An AI's internal simulation of how the world works, so it can imagine what happens next.
definitions.builder: Models that predict future observations given actions; used for robot planning and interactive video generation.
definitions.research: Learned dynamics models p(sₜ₊₁ | sₜ, aₜ) enabling planning or policy learning in imagination.

terms.analogy: Running the move in your head before making it.
terms.example: The robot used a world model to plan its grasp.

definitions.beginner: Training robots in a computer simulation, then getting the skills to work in the real world.
definitions.builder: Transferring policies trained in physics simulators to hardware via domain randomisation and fine-tuning.
definitions.research: Bridging the reality gap between simulated and physical dynamics and observations.

terms.analogy: Flight simulator hours before flying a real plane.
terms.example: Sim-to-real let the robot hand learn in days, not years.

definitions.beginner: A robot brain that sees, understands instructions and decides how to move.
definitions.builder: Extends a VLM to output robot actions; one model handles "pick up the red cup" from camera to motor commands.
definitions.research: Policies mapping visual observations and language goals to action tokens, pre-trained on web data plus robot demos.

terms.analogy: Eyes, ears and hands wired to the same brain.
terms.example: The VLA folded laundry it had never seen.

definitions.beginner: One general AI that can control many kinds of robots and learn new tasks quickly.
definitions.builder: Large cross-embodiment policies trained on pooled robot data, then fine-tuned for specific arms or humanoids.
definitions.research: Generalist policies exploiting scale across embodiments and tasks, analogous to LLM pre-training.

terms.analogy: A universal driving instructor for any vehicle.
terms.example: The humanoid startup licensed a robot foundation model.

definitions.beginner: A robot shaped like a person, with arms, legs and hands, so it can work in human spaces.
definitions.builder: Bipedal general-purpose robots betting that the human form fits existing workplaces; hardware cost and reliability are the hurdles.
definitions.research: Anthropomorphic platforms whose high-DoF control problems now lean on learned whole-body policies.

terms.analogy: A worker built for a world designed for humans.
terms.example: The factory is piloting a humanoid robot on the night shift.

definitions.beginner: Research that opens up AI models to understand exactly how they work inside.
definitions.builder: Reverse-engineering features and circuits inside networks, used to audit behaviour and debug safety issues.
definitions.research: Identifying human-interpretable features and causal circuits in activations, via probing, patching and dictionary learning.

terms.analogy: Neuroscience for neural networks.
terms.example: Mechanistic interpretability found the feature for "deception".

definitions.beginner: When a model packs more ideas into its neurons than it has neurons, so each neuron means several things.
definitions.builder: Why single neurons are hard to interpret; features overlap and must be untangled with tools like sparse autoencoders.
definitions.research: Representing more sparse features than dimensions via nearly orthogonal directions, at the cost of interference.

terms.analogy: Many radio stations sharing the same frequencies.
terms.example: Superposition explains why one neuron fires for both cats and cars.

definitions.beginner: A tool that untangles a model's internal signals into separate, understandable concepts.
definitions.builder: Trained on activations to decompose them into a large dictionary of sparsely active, interpretable features.
definitions.research: Dictionary learning with an L1-sparsity objective recovering monosemantic directions from superposed representations.

terms.analogy: Separating a smoothie back into its fruits.
terms.example: The sparse autoencoder found a Golden Gate Bridge feature.

definitions.beginner: Nudging an AI's behaviour by directly tweaking its internal signals instead of retraining it.
definitions.builder: Adding a feature direction to activations at inference to dial up or down a concept or behaviour.
definitions.research: Intervening on residual-stream activations along learned or contrastive directions to causally modulate outputs.

terms.analogy: Turning a specific knob inside the brain.
terms.example: Activation steering made the model obsessed with bridges.

definitions.beginner: Whether an AI's shown reasoning really reflects how it reached its answer.
definitions.builder: Reasoning traces can omit or rationalise the real cause of an answer; don't treat them as a reliable audit log.
definitions.research: The degree to which verbalised reasoning causally reflects the computation producing the output, measured via interventions.

terms.analogy: Does the student's working match how they actually solved it?
terms.example: CoT faithfulness tests found the model hid its use of a hint.

definitions.beginner: Asking an AI to do a task with no examples, just instructions.
definitions.builder: Prompting with only a task description; modern instruction-tuned models handle most tasks this way before you reach for examples.
definitions.research: Task performance without in-context demonstrations, relying on instruction tuning to map task descriptions to behaviour.

terms.analogy: Handing someone a task with no sample to copy.
terms.example: Zero-shot prompting was enough to classify the tickets.

definitions.beginner: An app you talk to in plain language that answers back, like ChatGPT or Claude.
definitions.builder: A conversational UI over an LLM with a system prompt, history management and often tools or retrieval behind it.
definitions.research: A dialogue system; modern ones are post-trained LLMs conditioned on multi-turn conversation transcripts.

terms.analogy: A help desk that never sleeps.
terms.example: The bank's new chatbot actually solved my problem.

definitions.beginner: When a long AI conversation slowly loses track of the original goal or instructions.
definitions.builder: Quality decay over long sessions as early instructions get diluted; fix with summaries, reminders and fresh context.
definitions.research: Degradation of instruction adherence with context length as attention to early tokens weakens relative to recent ones.

terms.analogy: A game of telephone with yourself.
terms.example: After 50 messages, context drift made it forget our style guide.

definitions.beginner: A setting that makes an AI reply in a tidy, machine-readable format instead of chatty text.
definitions.builder: Forces syntactically valid JSON output; pair with a schema (structured outputs) so fields are also guaranteed.
definitions.research: Constrained decoding restricted to the JSON grammar, without necessarily enforcing a specific schema.

terms.analogy: Asking for a filled-in form, not a letter.
terms.example: Turn on JSON mode so the app can read the answer.

definitions.beginner: How often an AI makes things up, measured as a percentage of answers.
definitions.builder: Share of responses with unsupported claims on a fixed eval set; track it per release and per feature.
definitions.research: Frequency of factually unsupported generations under a defined annotation protocol, sensitive to task and grader.

terms.analogy: A newspaper's corrections count.
terms.example: RAG cut our hallucination rate from 12% to 3%.

definitions.beginner: A setting that makes an AI choose only from its most likely next words, keeping answers sensible.
definitions.builder: Nucleus sampling, which keeps the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities sum to p; usually tune it or temperature, not both.
definitions.research: Truncating the predictive distribution to the minimal-mass nucleus ≥ p, then renormalising and sampling.

terms.analogy: Only picking from the top shelf.
terms.example: We set top-p sampling to 0.9 for the story generator.

definitions.beginner: A company's collection of documents and FAQs that an AI can search to answer questions.
definitions.builder: The curated source corpus behind RAG; its freshness and structure matter more than the model you choose.
definitions.research: A document or fact store serving as non-parametric memory for retrieval-augmented systems.

terms.analogy: The company handbook the assistant can open.
terms.example: We connected the bot to our knowledge base.

definitions.beginner: Methods that help people understand why an AI made a particular decision.
definitions.builder: Attribution, feature importance and rationales that make model decisions auditable; often required in finance and health.
definitions.research: Post-hoc and intrinsic interpretability techniques (SHAP, saliency, counterfactuals) explaining model predictions.

terms.analogy: Showing your working, not just the answer.
terms.example: Regulators asked for explainable AI before approving the loan model.

definitions.beginner: Thousands of AI chips wired together to work as one giant computer.
definitions.builder: Racks of GPUs joined by fast networking (NVLink, InfiniBand); training jobs span the whole cluster.
definitions.research: Distributed accelerator systems whose interconnect bandwidth and topology bound parallel training efficiency.

terms.analogy: An orchestra of chips playing one piece.
terms.example: The GPU cluster has 100,000 chips.

definitions.beginner: Making AI models smaller and faster so they're cheaper to run or fit on phones.
definitions.builder: Umbrella for quantization, pruning and distillation, trading a little quality for big cuts in memory and latency.
definitions.research: Techniques reducing parameter count or precision while bounding degradation in task loss.

terms.analogy: Packing a suitcase with vacuum bags.
terms.example: Model compression got it running on a phone.

definitions.beginner: Teaching AI with examples that come with the right answers attached.
definitions.builder: Training on labelled input→output pairs; classic for classifiers and the basis of supervised fine-tuning (SFT).
definitions.research: Learning a mapping from x to y by minimising loss over labelled pairs drawn from a joint distribution.

terms.analogy: Flashcards with the answer on the back.
terms.example: Supervised learning trained it on photos labelled "cat" or "dog".

definitions.beginner: AI finding patterns in data on its own, without being told the right answers.
definitions.builder: Learning structure from unlabelled data (clustering, embeddings); LLM pre-training is its self-supervised cousin.
definitions.research: Modelling p(x) or latent structure without targets, including clustering, density estimation and representation learning.

terms.analogy: Sorting a pile of photos without any labels.
terms.example: Unsupervised learning grouped customers into five types.

definitions.beginner: Teaching AI through trial and error, rewarding good results and discouraging bad ones.
definitions.builder: An agent optimises actions to maximise reward; used for RLHF and for training reasoning models on checkable tasks.
definitions.research: Learning a policy π(a|s) maximising expected discounted return through interaction with an environment.

terms.analogy: Training a dog with treats.
terms.example: Reinforcement learning taught it to win at Go.

definitions.beginner: When a model is too simple or undertrained to learn the patterns, so it does badly everywhere.
definitions.builder: High training and validation loss; fix with a bigger model, more training or better features.
definitions.research: High bias: the hypothesis class or optimisation can't capture the target function's structure.

terms.analogy: Skimming the textbook the night before.
terms.example: The tiny model was underfitting, so we scaled it up.

definitions.beginner: Automatically copying large amounts of content from websites to train AI.
definitions.builder: Crawling the web (e.g. Common Crawl) for training corpora; raises consent, copyright and robots.txt questions.
definitions.research: Large-scale automated collection of web data, with filtering and deduplication pipelines determining corpus quality.

terms.analogy: Photocopying the whole internet.
terms.example: News sites sued over data scraping for training.

definitions.beginner: People tagging examples with the right answer, like marking photos "cat", so AI can learn from them.
definitions.builder: Human annotation for supervised training and evals; expert labellers now write reasoning traces and preference rankings.
definitions.research: Producing targets or judgements for training data, where annotator agreement and guidelines shape label noise.

terms.analogy: Writing the answer key.
terms.example: Data labeling is now done by PhDs for frontier models.

definitions.beginner: An AI agent that works toward a goal for a long time with little or no human help.
definitions.builder: Long-running agents with broad tool access that plan and recover from errors on their own; need strong guardrails and audit logs.
definitions.research: Agents operating over extended horizons with minimal oversight, where error compounding and goal robustness dominate.

terms.analogy: An employee working remotely all week without check-ins.
terms.example: The autonomous agent ran overnight and fixed 30 bugs.

definitions.beginner: When an AI asks your app to run a specific function, like "get_weather", with the right details filled in.
definitions.builder: The model emits a structured call matching your declared JSON schema; your code executes it and returns the result.
definitions.research: Structured action emission over a typed API surface, enabling programmatic execution of model-selected operations.

terms.analogy: Filling in an order form for the kitchen.
terms.example: Function calling lets the bot look up your order status.

definitions.beginner: Finding items by how similar their meaning is, using lists of numbers that represent them.
definitions.builder: Nearest-neighbour search over embeddings, usually approximate (HNSW) for speed at scale.
definitions.research: k-NN retrieval in embedding space under a similarity metric, approximated with graph or quantisation indexes.

terms.analogy: Finding songs that "sound like" this one.
terms.example: Vector search found articles about refunds even without the word.

definitions.beginner: Tailoring what an AI shows or says to each person's preferences and history.
definitions.builder: Feeding user profile, memory and behaviour into prompts or ranking so outputs fit each user.
definitions.research: Conditioning models on user-specific signals, balancing relevance gains against privacy and filter-bubble risks.

terms.analogy: A barista who remembers your order.
terms.example: Personalization made the tutor start at my level.

definitions.beginner: The standing rules you give an AI about how to behave, like tone, role or what to avoid.
definitions.builder: Persistent instructions (system prompt, custom instructions) that apply to every turn; keep them clear and testable.
definitions.research: High-priority conditioning text that post-training teaches models to follow over conflicting user requests.

terms.analogy: The house rules on the fridge.
terms.example: Our system instructions say to always answer in British English.

definitions.beginner: When you give an AI more text than it can hold in memory, so some gets cut off or rejected.
definitions.builder: Exceeding the context window; handle with truncation, summarising, compaction or retrieval instead of pasting everything.
definitions.research: Inputs exceeding the model's maximum sequence length, requiring eviction or compression strategies.

terms.analogy: Overfilling a cup.
terms.example: The 900-page PDF caused a context overflow.

definitions.beginner: Caps on how many requests you can send to an AI service in a given time.
definitions.builder: Requests- and tokens-per-minute quotas; handle 429 errors with retries, backoff and queues.
definitions.research: Admission control on shared inference capacity to bound tail latency and ensure fair allocation.

terms.analogy: A one-in, one-out door policy.
terms.example: Rate limiting kicked in during our launch spike.

definitions.beginner: The maximum amount of text, counted in tokens, an AI can read or write in one go.
definitions.builder: Context window plus the max output tokens setting; cut-off answers usually mean max_tokens was too low.
definitions.research: Hard bounds on input and generated sequence length imposed by architecture and serving configuration.

terms.analogy: A word count on an essay.
terms.example: The summary stopped mid-sentence because it hit the token limit.

definitions.beginner: A chain of steps, like fetch, clean, ask the AI, check, save, that turns input into a finished result.
definitions.builder: A fixed workflow of model calls and code; more predictable and cheaper than open-ended agents.
definitions.research: A directed composition of model and non-model stages with explicit data flow and validation.

terms.analogy: An assembly line.
terms.example: Our AI pipeline turns call recordings into CRM notes.

definitions.beginner: The rules, policies and oversight an organisation or government uses to manage AI responsibly.
definitions.builder: Inventories, risk reviews, approval flows and monitoring for AI systems; increasingly required by law and customers.
definitions.research: Institutional mechanisms (standards, audits, liability) shaping AI development and deployment.

terms.analogy: A company's rulebook for using powerful tools.
terms.example: The board set up an AI governance committee.

definitions.beginner: A catalogue that keeps track of every AI model a team has built, with versions and notes.
definitions.builder: Versioned store of models with metadata, eval results and approval status; the source of truth for what's deployed.
definitions.research: An artifact store linking model versions to lineage, data and evaluation for reproducibility.

terms.analogy: A library catalogue for models.
terms.example: Pull the approved version from the model registry.

definitions.beginner: Data a company collects but never uses, like old emails, call recordings and PDFs.
definitions.builder: Unstructured, unindexed internal data that LLMs can now parse; often the most valuable RAG source.
definitions.research: Latent organisational data lacking structure or metadata, newly tractable with foundation-model extraction.

terms.analogy: Boxes in the attic you forgot you had.
terms.example: Ten years of support calls were dark data until now.

definitions.beginner: A loop where more users create more data, which improves the AI, which attracts more users.
definitions.builder: Logging usage and feedback to improve prompts, evals and fine-tunes; a common AI moat.
definitions.research: A positive feedback loop between deployment data and model quality.

terms.analogy: A snowball rolling downhill.
terms.example: Their data flywheel is why the product keeps getting better.

definitions.beginner: A score of how similar two pieces of text are in meaning, from -1 to 1.
definitions.builder: The default metric for comparing embeddings; the angle between vectors, ignoring their length.
definitions.research: cos θ = a·b / (‖a‖‖b‖); equivalent to dot product for unit-normalised vectors.

terms.analogy: Checking if two arrows point the same way.
terms.example: Cosine similarity ranked the closest help articles.

definitions.beginner: Splitting documents at natural topic breaks instead of every fixed number of words.
definitions.builder: Chunk boundaries chosen by headings or embedding shifts, so each chunk holds one idea; improves retrieval precision.
definitions.research: Segmentation using semantic discontinuities between adjacent sentence embeddings rather than fixed windows.

terms.analogy: Cutting a cake along the layers.
terms.example: Semantic chunking kept each policy section intact.

definitions.beginner: Letting neighbouring document pieces share a few sentences so no idea gets cut in half.
definitions.builder: Repeating 10–20% of tokens between consecutive chunks to preserve context across boundaries.
definitions.research: Sliding-window segmentation with stride smaller than window size, trading index size for boundary recall.

terms.analogy: Overlapping roof tiles so rain can't slip through.
terms.example: Adding chunk overlap fixed answers that missed half a sentence.

definitions.beginner: A fast way of searching millions of vectors by hopping through a layered map of neighbours.
definitions.builder: The most common approximate nearest-neighbour index in vector databases; tune M and ef for recall vs speed.
definitions.research: Multi-layer proximity graphs with greedy search giving logarithmic-ish ANN query complexity.

terms.analogy: Taking motorways first, then side streets.
terms.example: HNSW returns results in milliseconds.

definitions.beginner: RAG that builds a map of people, places and ideas from your documents so the AI can connect the dots.
definitions.builder: Extract entities and relations into a knowledge graph, summarise communities, then retrieve over the graph for global questions.
definitions.research: Graph-structured retrieval enabling multi-hop and corpus-level query answering beyond chunk similarity.

terms.analogy: A detective's string board instead of a pile of notes.
terms.example: GraphRAG answered "what themes connect all these reports?"

definitions.beginner: A network of facts showing how things relate, like "Paris is the capital of France".
definitions.builder: Entities and typed relationships queried alongside vector search to ground answers in structured facts.
definitions.research: A labelled directed graph of (subject, predicate, object) triples supporting symbolic reasoning over relations.

terms.analogy: A family tree for facts.
terms.example: The knowledge graph knows which products share a supplier.

definitions.beginner: Organising stored vectors so similar ones can be found quickly.
definitions.builder: Building ANN structures (HNSW, IVF, PQ) over embeddings; trades memory, build time and recall.
definitions.research: Data structures for sublinear approximate similarity search via graphs, partitions or quantisation.

terms.analogy: Shelving a library so you don't scan every book.
terms.example: Re-running vector indexing took an hour for 50M docs.

definitions.beginner: Two ways to search, by meaning (dense) or by exact keywords (sparse).
definitions.builder: Dense uses embeddings and catches paraphrases; sparse (BM25) nails exact terms and IDs. Hybrid combines both.
definitions.research: Learned continuous representations versus high-dimensional lexical vectors, with complementary recall profiles.

terms.analogy: A friend who gets what you mean versus an index that matches exact words.
terms.example: Dense vs. sparse retrieval each missed things the other caught.

definitions.beginner: Narrowing a search by facts like date, author or product before matching on meaning.
definitions.builder: Pre- or post-filtering vector results by structured fields; essential for permissions and freshness.
definitions.research: Constrained ANN search combining attribute predicates with similarity ranking.

terms.analogy: Only searching this year's folder.
terms.example: Metadata filtering hides docs the user isn't allowed to see.

definitions.beginner: Trimming retrieved documents to just the useful bits before giving them to the AI.
definitions.builder: Extract or summarise relevant spans from retrieved chunks to cut tokens and noise.
definitions.research: Query-aware selection or abstraction of retrieved text to maximise information per token.

terms.analogy: Highlighting the key lines before handing over the report.
terms.example: Context compression cut our prompt from 20k to 4k tokens.

definitions.beginner: Customising a big model by training only a tiny part of it, saving time and money.
definitions.builder: Family of methods (LoRA, adapters, prefix tuning) that update a small fraction of parameters.
definitions.research: Fine-tuning restricted to a low-dimensional parameter subspace or added modules, with frozen base weights.

terms.analogy: Tailoring a suit instead of sewing a new one.
terms.example: PEFT let us fine-tune on a single GPU.

definitions.beginner: A way to fine-tune huge models on modest hardware by compressing the base model first.
definitions.builder: LoRA adapters trained on top of a 4-bit quantized frozen base; fine-tune a 65B model on one GPU.
definitions.research: Backprop through a 4-bit NormalFloat-quantised base into low-rank adapters, with paged optimisers.

terms.analogy: Renovating a room while the house is vacuum-packed.
