terms.example: QLoRA made the 70B fine-tune affordable.

definitions.beginner: Training an AI using another AI's ratings instead of only humans'.
definitions.builder: An AI labeller generates preference data at scale, often guided by principles; cheaper than human RLHF.
definitions.research: Preference optimisation with model-generated comparisons, as in Constitutional AI.

terms.analogy: A senior student grading practice papers.
terms.example: RLAIF scaled preference data a hundredfold.

definitions.beginner: Training a model on example conversations showing exactly how it should respond.
definitions.builder: Fine-tuning on curated prompt→ideal-response pairs; usually the first post-training step before preference tuning.
definitions.research: Maximum-likelihood training on demonstration data, cloning a target behaviour policy.

terms.analogy: Learning by copying model answers.
terms.example: SFT taught the base model to follow instructions.

definitions.beginner: When training a model on something new makes it forget what it knew before.
definitions.builder: Fine-tuning erodes general abilities; mitigate with LoRA, mixing in general data and low learning rates.
definitions.research: Interference in shared parameters when sequentially optimising on shifted distributions.

terms.analogy: Learning Spanish and forgetting your French.
terms.example: Catastrophic forgetting made the legal fine-tune bad at maths.

definitions.beginner: A plan that changes how big the model's learning steps are over the course of training.
definitions.builder: Warmup then decay (cosine, linear, WSD); a bad schedule wastes compute or causes divergence.
definitions.research: Time-varying step-size policy η(t) shaping optimisation dynamics and final loss.

terms.analogy: Sprinting at the start, then slowing to a careful walk.
terms.example: The learning rate scheduler warms up over the first 2,000 steps.

definitions.beginner: How many examples a model looks at before each update.
definitions.builder: Bigger batches use hardware better and smooth gradients; LLM training ramps to millions of tokens per batch.
definitions.research: Mini-batch cardinality governing gradient noise scale and the critical batch size beyond which returns diminish.

terms.analogy: Grading a stack of papers before adjusting your teaching.
terms.example: Doubling the batch size halved training time.

definitions.beginner: A saved snapshot of a model during or after training.
definitions.builder: Weights plus optimiser state saved periodically so training can resume and the best version can ship.
definitions.research: Serialised parameter and optimiser state enabling fault tolerance and post-hoc model selection.

terms.analogy: A save point in a video game.
terms.example: We rolled back to yesterday's checkpoint.

definitions.beginner: Having an AI explore several lines of reasoning, like branches, and pick the best one.
definitions.builder: Generate multiple reasoning steps, evaluate them and search (BFS/DFS) over the tree; costly but strong on puzzles.
definitions.research: Deliberate search over intermediate thought states with model-based value estimates.

terms.analogy: A chess player considering several moves ahead.
terms.example: Tree-of-thoughts solved puzzles that chain-of-thought missed.

definitions.beginner: An agent pattern where the AI alternates between thinking and taking actions, like searching.
definitions.builder: Thought → action (tool call) → observation loops; the template behind most tool-using agents.
definitions.research: Interleaving reasoning traces with environment actions so observations update subsequent reasoning.

terms.analogy: Think, check, think again.
terms.example: The ReAct agent searched three times before answering.

definitions.beginner: Asking the AI the same question several times and going with the most common answer.
definitions.builder: Sample multiple reasoning paths and majority-vote the final answers; boosts accuracy at extra cost.
definitions.research: Marginalising over sampled reasoning chains by voting on final answers.

terms.analogy: Asking five friends and trusting the majority.
terms.example: Self-consistency fixed one in five maths errors.

definitions.beginner: Giving the AI small hints, like keywords, that steer it toward the answer you want.
definitions.builder: A small policy model generates hint keywords per input that are added to the prompt of a larger frozen model.
definitions.research: Learning instance-specific stimulus prompts via SFT and RL to guide black-box LLMs.

terms.analogy: A coach whispering keywords from the sidelines.
terms.example: Directional stimulus prompting improved summary coverage.

definitions.beginner: Having the AI write a quick outline first, then fill in each point at the same time to answer faster.
definitions.builder: Generate an answer skeleton, then expand points in parallel calls to cut end-to-end latency.
definitions.research: Parallel decoding via outline-then-expand, trading coherence for wall-clock speed.

terms.analogy: Drafting bullet points, then a team writes each paragraph.
terms.example: Skeleton-of-thought made long answers twice as fast.

definitions.beginner: Making the AI review and critique its own work, then improve it.
definitions.builder: Draft → critique → revise loop, optionally with tests or a separate critic model.
definitions.research: Self-refinement using model-generated feedback as an additional conditioning signal.

terms.analogy: Proofreading your own essay.
terms.example: The reflection pattern caught bugs before the code was shown.

definitions.beginner: A process where AI handles several steps of a job, deciding some of what to do along the way.
definitions.builder: Structured flows mixing fixed steps with model decisions (routing, reflection, tool use); the middle ground between pipelines and agents.
definitions.research: Hybrid control flows where models select among predefined operations within a bounded graph.

terms.analogy: A recipe with "season to taste" steps.
terms.example: Our agentic workflow drafts, checks and files each claim.

definitions.beginner: Picking just the right tools for an AI from a big toolbox, so it isn't overwhelmed.
definitions.builder: Searching a large tool catalogue and loading only relevant tool definitions into context.
definitions.research: Retrieval over tool descriptions to scale the action space without exhausting context.

terms.analogy: Handing a mechanic the wrenches for this car only.
terms.example: Tool retrieval let the agent use 400 tools.

definitions.beginner: Asking the AI to make a plan first, then carry it out step by step.
definitions.builder: A prompt pattern separating planning from execution; reduces skipped steps in multi-step tasks.
definitions.research: Decomposition prompting that elicits an explicit plan before stepwise execution.

terms.analogy: Writing the shopping list before going to the store.
terms.example: Plan-and-solve stopped it skipping steps.

definitions.beginner: Where an AI agent keeps notes on what it has done so it can pick up where it left off.
definitions.builder: Persistent state (scratchpad, conversation summary, task list) saved between steps or sessions.
definitions.research: External state persistence decoupling agent continuity from a single context window.

terms.analogy: A sticky note left for your future self.
terms.example: The memory buffer let the agent resume after a crash.

definitions.beginner: An agent's working memory for the current task versus what it remembers across days.
definitions.builder: Short-term lives in the context window; long-term is stored externally (files, vector DB) and retrieved when needed.
definitions.research: Partitioning agent state into transient context and persistent retrievable memory.

terms.analogy: Your desk versus your filing cabinet.
terms.example: Short-term vs. long-term memory explains why it forgot your name tomorrow.

definitions.beginner: Automatically sending each request to the best model or prompt for the job.
definitions.builder: A classifier or small model routes easy queries to cheap models and hard ones to strong models.
definitions.research: Learned routing over model/prompt ensembles optimising a quality–cost frontier.

terms.analogy: A hospital triage desk.
terms.example: Dynamic prompt routing cut costs by 60%.

definitions.beginner: Checking that an AI's answer has the exact fields and types your app expects.
definitions.builder: Parsing outputs into typed schemas (Pydantic, Instructor, Zod) and retrying on failure.
definitions.research: Runtime type-checking of generated structures against a schema, with repair loops on violation.

terms.analogy: A form that won't submit until it's filled in properly.
terms.example: Structured output validation caught a missing price field.

definitions.beginner: How long you wait before an AI's answer starts appearing.
definitions.builder: Latency until the first streamed token, dominated by prefill; the number users actually feel in chat UIs.
definitions.research: Prefill-bound latency scaling with prompt length and queueing delay before decode begins.

terms.analogy: How long before the waiter brings the first dish.
terms.example: Prompt caching halved our TTFT.

definitions.beginner: How fast an AI writes once it starts, measured in tokens each second.
definitions.builder: Decode speed per stream; drives how long full answers take and how many users a GPU can serve.
definitions.research: Autoregressive decode throughput, bounded by memory bandwidth for weights and KV cache.

terms.analogy: Typing speed.
terms.example: The small model runs at 200 tokens per second.

definitions.beginner: Popular open-source software for running AI models quickly on servers.
definitions.builder: High-throughput inference engine with PagedAttention, continuous batching and an OpenAI-compatible server.
definitions.research: A serving system co-designing KV-cache memory management and scheduling for LLM inference.

terms.analogy: A high-performance engine for model serving.
terms.example: We self-host Llama on vLLM.

definitions.beginner: An easy app for downloading and running AI models on your own laptop.
definitions.builder: A local model runner wrapping llama.cpp with one-line installs, a model library and a local API.
definitions.research: Developer tooling packaging quantised GGUF models for local CPU/GPU inference.

terms.analogy: An app store for local models.
terms.example: I run a coding model offline with Ollama.

definitions.beginner: Lightweight software that runs AI models on ordinary computers, even without a big GPU.
definitions.builder: C/C++ inference engine with aggressive quantization (GGUF format); powers most local AI tools.
definitions.research: CPU- and Apple-Silicon-optimised inference with integer quantisation kernels and memory-mapped weights.

terms.analogy: A model that fits in your backpack.
terms.example: llama.cpp runs a 7B model on a MacBook Air.

definitions.beginner: The extra wait when an AI server has to wake up and load the model first.
definitions.builder: Time to provision a GPU and load weights before serving; hurts serverless and scale-to-zero deployments.
definitions.research: Startup overhead from weight loading and kernel compilation, amortised by keeping replicas warm.

terms.analogy: A car on a frosty morning.
terms.example: Cold start latency made the first request take 40 seconds.

definitions.beginner: Removing parts of a model that barely matter, to make it smaller and faster.
definitions.builder: Zeroing or deleting low-importance weights, heads or layers, then briefly retraining to recover quality.
definitions.research: Structured or unstructured sparsification guided by magnitude or saliency criteria.

terms.analogy: Pruning a hedge.
terms.example: Model pruning removed a third of the layers.

definitions.beginner: Extra tokens you pay for that don't add value, like long boilerplate instructions or wordy answers.
definitions.builder: Bloat from verbose prompts, repeated context, tool schemas and padding; trim it to cut cost and latency.
definitions.research: Non-informative token mass in inputs and outputs that consumes compute without improving task performance.

terms.analogy: Packaging that costs more than the product.
terms.example: Our tool schemas were 40% token overhead.

definitions.beginner: Summarising older parts of a long conversation so it still fits in the AI's memory.
definitions.builder: Compaction of history (summaries, dropping stale tool output) so long-running agents keep going.
definitions.research: Lossy compression of the context state, trading fidelity for effective horizon length.

terms.analogy: Replacing old meeting notes with a one-page summary.
terms.example: Context window compression kept the agent running for hours.

definitions.beginner: A famous multiple-choice test covering 57 school and professional subjects.
definitions.builder: Broad knowledge benchmark, now saturated for frontier models; harder variants (MMLU-Pro) took over.
definitions.research: 57-subject multiple-choice benchmark measuring zero/few-shot knowledge breadth.

terms.analogy: A general knowledge exam.
terms.example: Every model now scores near 90 on MMLU.

definitions.beginner: A test of whether AI can write small working programs.
definitions.builder: 164 Python function problems checked by unit tests (pass@k); a classic coding benchmark now largely saturated.
definitions.research: Execution-based functional-correctness evaluation of code synthesis from docstrings.

terms.analogy: A coding interview with an automated grader.
terms.example: It scores 95% on HumanEval but still struggles in real repos.

definitions.beginner: A test of 8,000 grade-school maths word problems.
definitions.builder: Multi-step arithmetic reasoning benchmark; popularised chain-of-thought, now saturated.
definitions.research: Grade-school maths dataset evaluating multi-step numerical reasoning with exact-match answers.

terms.analogy: A primary school maths homework sheet.
terms.example: Chain-of-thought pushed GSM8K scores past 90%.

definitions.beginner: A public website where people vote on which of two anonymous AIs answered better.
definitions.builder: Crowdsourced pairwise votes turned into Elo-style leaderboard ratings; reflects user preference, can reward style.
definitions.research: Bradley–Terry ratings fit to blind pairwise human preferences (LMSYS/LMArena).

terms.analogy: A blind taste test.
terms.example: The new model jumped to first on Chatbot Arena.

definitions.beginner: A score that goes up when you beat strong opponents, used to rank AI models like chess players.
definitions.builder: Pairwise-comparison rating system behind arena leaderboards; differences map to win probabilities.
definitions.research: Logistic rating model where rating gaps predict expected win rates.

terms.analogy: Chess rankings for chatbots.
terms.example: A 100-point Elo rating gap means about 64% win rate.

definitions.beginner: Tools that score how well a RAG system finds and uses the right information.
definitions.builder: RAG eval frameworks (Ragas, TruLens) computing faithfulness, relevance and context precision/recall with LLM judges.
definitions.research: Reference-free metric suites decomposing RAG quality into retrieval and generation components.

terms.analogy: A report card for search-plus-answer bots.
terms.example: Ragas showed retrieval, not the model, was the weak link.

definitions.beginner: Whether an AI's answer sticks to what the source documents actually say.
definitions.builder: Share of claims supported by retrieved context; the key RAG anti-hallucination metric.
definitions.research: Entailment of generated statements by provided evidence, estimated via NLI or LLM judges.

terms.analogy: A reporter who quotes sources accurately.
terms.example: Faithfulness dropped when we allowed outside knowledge.

definitions.beginner: Whether the AI actually answered the question that was asked.
definitions.builder: Scores how directly a response addresses the query, independent of factual accuracy.
definitions.research: Semantic alignment between question and answer, often via reverse-generated questions.

terms.analogy: Did they answer what you asked, or something nearby?
terms.example: Answer relevance flagged replies that rambled.

definitions.beginner: Whether search found the right documents (recall) without lots of junk (precision).
definitions.builder: Retrieval metrics: share of retrieved chunks that are relevant, and share of needed info that was retrieved.
definitions.research: Precision and recall of the retrieved set against ground-truth evidence for each query.

terms.analogy: Did you grab all the right files, and only the right files?
terms.example: Context precision / recall showed the retriever missed key policies.

definitions.beginner: Old-school scores that compare AI text with a reference by counting shared words.
definitions.builder: N-gram overlap metrics for translation (BLEU) and summaries (ROUGE); cheap but weak judges of quality for LLMs.
definitions.research: Precision- and recall-oriented n-gram overlap statistics against reference texts.

terms.analogy: Grading an essay by matching words to the answer key.
terms.example: BLEU / ROUGE scores rewarded copying, not quality.

definitions.beginner: Precision is how many flagged items were right; recall is how many right items got flagged.
definitions.builder: Precision = TP/(TP+FP), recall = TP/(TP+FN); pick the trade-off your product can live with.
definitions.research: Complementary classification metrics whose trade-off is traced by varying the decision threshold.

terms.analogy: A fishing net: catch only fish, or catch every fish?
terms.example: The spam filter favours precision vs. recall to protect real emails.

definitions.beginner: A single number that balances precision and recall.
definitions.builder: Harmonic mean of precision and recall; useful for imbalanced classification evals.
definitions.research: F1 = 2PR/(P+R), the harmonic mean penalising imbalance between precision and recall.

terms.analogy: One grade for both accuracy and completeness.
terms.example: The classifier's F1 score rose to 0.91.

definitions.beginner: A table showing what a model predicted versus what was actually true.
definitions.builder: Counts of true/false positives and negatives per class; reveals which categories get mixed up.
definitions.research: Cross-tabulation of predicted and true labels from which classification metrics are derived.

terms.analogy: A scoreboard of right and wrong guesses.
terms.example: The confusion matrix showed refunds mislabelled as complaints.

definitions.beginner: Showing two versions of a prompt to different users to see which works better.
definitions.builder: Online experiments comparing prompts or models on real metrics (resolution rate, thumbs-up), after offline evals.
definitions.research: Randomised controlled comparison of prompt variants under live traffic with significance testing.

terms.analogy: Two shop signs, see which brings more customers.
terms.example: A/B testing prompts showed the shorter one converted better.

definitions.beginner: When an AI gets worse over time because the world, or the data it sees, changes.
definitions.builder: Monitor input distributions and quality metrics in production; alert, re-evaluate and retrain when they shift.
definitions.research: Performance degradation from covariate or concept shift between training and deployment distributions.

terms.analogy: A map that slowly goes out of date.
terms.example: Model drift crept in after we launched in a new country.

definitions.beginner: Inputs that look very different from anything the AI saw in training.
definitions.builder: Where models fail unpredictably; test with edge cases, new domains and adversarial inputs.
definitions.research: Samples from a distribution differing from the training distribution, where generalisation guarantees lapse.

terms.analogy: A tourist in a country they never studied.
terms.example: Handwritten forms were out-of-distribution for the OCR model.

definitions.beginner: Using AI to attack other AI systems automatically to find weaknesses at scale.
definitions.builder: Attacker models generate and mutate jailbreaks and harmful prompts; findings feed safety training and evals.
definitions.research: Adversarial search over the input space with RL-trained or prompted attacker models.

terms.analogy: A robot sparring partner.
terms.example: Automated red teaming found 2,000 jailbreaks overnight.

definitions.beginner: A small AI that screens inputs and outputs for harmful content, like Llama Guard.
definitions.builder: Moderation models (Llama Guard, NeMo Guardrails) wrapped around an LLM to block unsafe requests and responses.
definitions.research: Discriminative policy models classifying content against a harm taxonomy, layered with generation.

terms.analogy: Airport security for chatbots.
terms.example: A safety classifier blocks requests for weapons instructions.

definitions.beginner: How many different tokens a model knows, often 50,000 to 250,000.
definitions.builder: Bigger vocabularies compress text into fewer tokens (cheaper, multilingual) but enlarge the embedding tables.
definitions.research: |V| trades sequence length against embedding/softmax parameter cost and rare-token undertraining.

terms.analogy: How many Lego brick shapes are in the box.
terms.example: The bigger vocabulary size made Hindi much cheaper.

definitions.beginner: A way of splitting words into pieces, used by Google's BERT.
definitions.builder: Subword tokenizer that merges pairs maximising training-data likelihood; marks continuations with "##".
definitions.research: Likelihood-guided greedy merge segmentation, a close relative of BPE.

terms.analogy: Breaking "unhappiness" into "un", "##happi", "##ness".
terms.example: BERT uses WordPiece tokens.

definitions.beginner: A tokenizer that works directly on raw text in any language, including spaces.
definitions.builder: Language-agnostic tokenizer library (BPE or unigram) treating whitespace as a symbol; used by Llama and T5.
definitions.research: Lossless subword tokenisation over raw Unicode streams without pre-tokenisation.

terms.analogy: A universal cutter for any language's text.
terms.example: SentencePiece handles Japanese without word spaces.

definitions.beginner: A tokenizer that keeps the most useful word pieces by probability.
definitions.builder: Starts with a large vocabulary and prunes pieces that least hurt likelihood; supports sampling multiple segmentations.
definitions.research: Unigram language model over subwords optimised via EM, with vocabulary pruning by loss contribution.

terms.analogy: Keeping only the most-used puzzle pieces.
terms.example: Unigram tokenization is an option in SentencePiece.

definitions.beginner: How many numbers are in each embedding vector, like 768 or 3,072.
definitions.builder: Higher dimensions capture more nuance but cost more storage and search time; Matryoshka embeddings can be truncated.
definitions.research: Dimensionality d of the representation space, bounding capacity and ANN cost.

terms.analogy: How many adjectives you get to describe a thing.
terms.example: We shrank the embedding dimension to 512 to save storage.

definitions.beginner: A filter telling the model which words it's allowed to look at.
definitions.builder: Blocks padding tokens and, in causal models, future tokens so predictions only use the past.
definitions.research: Additive −∞ masking of attention logits enforcing causality or ignoring padding.

terms.analogy: Covering the answers while you read the question.
terms.example: The causal attention mask stops it peeking ahead.

definitions.beginner: A way of telling a model about word distance by penalising far-away words.
definitions.builder: Adds a distance-proportional penalty to attention scores instead of position embeddings; extrapolates to longer inputs.
definitions.research: Head-specific linear biases −m·|i−j| on attention logits enabling length extrapolation.

terms.analogy: Voices get quieter the further away they are.
terms.example: ALiBi let the model read past its training length.

definitions.beginner: Dense models use every part for every word; sparse models only switch on some parts.
definitions.builder: MoE (sparse) models get big-model quality at lower per-token compute but need more memory.
definitions.research: Conditional computation versus full parameter activation per token, with distinct scaling behaviour.

terms.analogy: Everyone works every shift versus specialists on call.
terms.example: The sparse vs. dense models debate is about memory versus compute.

definitions.beginner: The part of a mixture-of-experts model that decides which experts handle each word.
definitions.builder: A small learned layer scoring experts per token and picking the top-k; load balancing keeps experts evenly used.
definitions.research: A gating function softmax(W·x) selecting experts, regularised with auxiliary balance losses.

terms.analogy: A receptionist sending patients to specialists.
terms.example: The router sends maths tokens to the same few experts.

definitions.beginner: A memory-saving attention design where all heads share the same keys and values.
definitions.builder: One shared K/V head across query heads; shrinks the KV cache and speeds decoding with small quality loss.
definitions.research: Attention with H query heads and a single key/value head, cutting memory bandwidth at decode.

terms.analogy: Many readers sharing one reference book.
terms.example: MQA made long-context serving affordable.

definitions.beginner: How each word in a sentence looks at all the other words to understand its meaning.
definitions.builder: Each token builds query, key and value vectors; queries match keys to decide how much of each value to mix in.
definitions.research: Attention where Q = XW_Q, K = XW_K, V = XW_V all derive from the same sequence X.

terms.analogy: Everyone at a table listening for the comments relevant to them.
terms.example: Self-attention links "it" to "the server" in the sentence.

definitions.beginner: The core maths formula a transformer uses to decide what to pay attention to.
definitions.builder: softmax(QKᵀ/√d)V; the √d scaling keeps scores from saturating the softmax.
definitions.research: Dot-product similarity scaled by 1/√d_k to stabilise variance, normalised with softmax over keys.

terms.analogy: Scoring how well each key fits your question, then blending answers.
terms.example: FlashAttention computes scaled dot-product attention without storing the full matrix.

definitions.beginner: Running several attention processes side by side, each noticing different relationships.
definitions.builder: Splits the model dimension into heads with separate Q/K/V projections, then concatenates outputs.
definitions.research: Parallel attention in h subspaces, letting heads specialise (syntax, position, induction).

terms.analogy: Several highlighters, each marking something different.
terms.example: Multi-head attention lets one head track grammar and another track names.

definitions.beginner: A middle ground where groups of attention heads share memory to run faster.
definitions.builder: Query heads share K/V within groups; most of MHA's quality with most of MQA's KV-cache savings.
definitions.research: Interpolation between MHA and MQA with G key-value heads, uptrainable from MHA checkpoints.

terms.analogy: Study groups sharing one textbook per table.
terms.example: Llama uses GQA to cut KV cache memory.

definitions.beginner: A transformer design with one part that reads the input and another that writes the output.
definitions.builder: The original transformer layout, used by T5 and translation models; most chat LLMs are decoder-only.
definitions.research: Bidirectional encoder plus autoregressive decoder connected by cross-attention over encoder states.

terms.analogy: A listener and a speaker working as a pair.
terms.example: Translation models often use an encoder-decoder design.

definitions.beginner: Training an AI to guess the next word using only the words before it.
definitions.builder: The next-token prediction objective behind GPT-style models, enforced with a causal mask.
definitions.research: Maximising Σ log p(xₜ | x<t) under left-to-right factorisation.

terms.analogy: Finishing someone's sentence.
terms.example: Causal language modeling is how chat models are pre-trained.

definitions.beginner: Training an AI by hiding random words in a sentence and asking it to fill the gaps.
definitions.builder: BERT's objective; good for understanding and embeddings, not for generating text.
definitions.research: Denoising objective predicting masked tokens from bidirectional context.

terms.analogy: A fill-in-the-blanks worksheet.
terms.example: Masked language modeling made BERT great at search.

definitions.beginner: Shortcuts that let information skip past layers, making very deep networks trainable.
definitions.builder: Each block adds its output to its input (x + f(x)); keeps gradients healthy across hundreds of layers.
definitions.research: Identity skip paths forming a residual stream that layers read from and write to additively.

terms.analogy: An express lane past the traffic.
terms.example: Residual connections let us train 100-layer models.

definitions.beginner: A step that rescales numbers inside a model to keep training stable.
definitions.builder: Normalises each token's activations; Pre-LN (before each block) trains more stably than the original Post-LN.
definitions.research: Per-sample normalisation to zero mean and unit variance with learned gain and bias.

terms.analogy: Adjusting the volume so no instrument drowns out the rest.
terms.example: Switching to Pre-LN layer normalization stopped the loss spikes.

definitions.beginner: A simpler, faster version of layer normalization used in most new models.
definitions.builder: Scales by root-mean-square only, with no mean subtraction or bias; cheaper and equally stable.
definitions.research: x / RMS(x) · g, dropping re-centring from LayerNorm.

terms.analogy: Adjusting volume without re-tuning the instrument.
terms.example: Llama replaced LayerNorm with RMSNorm.

definitions.beginner: A modern math function inside model layers that helps them learn better.
definitions.builder: Gated feed-forward activation (Swish × linear gate) used in Llama, PaLM and most recent LLMs.
definitions.research: FFN(x) = (Swish(xW) ⊙ xV)W₂, a gated linear unit variant with better quality per FLOP.

terms.analogy: A dimmer switch on each signal.
terms.example: Swapping in SwiGLU improved perplexity.

definitions.beginner: A smooth on/off function that decides how much signal passes through each neuron.
definitions.builder: The activation in BERT and GPT-2; smoother than ReLU, since largely replaced by SwiGLU.
definitions.research: x·Φ(x), weighting inputs by the Gaussian CDF.

terms.analogy: A soft valve rather than a hard switch.
terms.example: GPT-2 uses GELU activations.

definitions.beginner: An alternative to transformers that reads text like a stream, using memory that doesn't grow with length.
definitions.builder: Linear-time sequence models (S4, Mamba) with constant-size state; fast on long inputs, often hybridised with attention.
definitions.research: Discretised linear dynamical systems h' = Ah + Bx, y = Ch, computed as convolutions or scans.

terms.analogy: Taking running notes instead of rereading the whole book.
terms.example: The state space model handles million-token audio.

definitions.beginner: A fast AI architecture that rivals transformers on long text by remembering selectively.
definitions.builder: Selective SSM with input-dependent parameters and a hardware-aware scan; linear scaling, used in hybrids like Jamba.
definitions.research: SSM with data-dependent (B, C, Δ), enabling content-based selection while retaining recurrent inference.

terms.analogy: A reader who decides what's worth remembering.
terms.example: The hybrid model mixes Mamba layers with attention.

definitions.beginner: A design that routes heavy thinking through a small set of internal "latent" slots for efficient image generation.
definitions.builder: Splits computation between data tokens and a smaller latent set, reading and writing across them; efficient for diffusion.
definitions.research: Adaptive computation via latent tokens with cross-attention read/write to the interface, recurrently across diffusion steps.

terms.analogy: A small committee summarising a huge crowd.
terms.example: Recurrent interface networks generated high-res images efficiently.

definitions.beginner: Small, adaptable networks inspired by worm brains that keep adjusting to changing inputs.
definitions.builder: Continuous-time recurrent models with input-dependent time constants; compact and strong on control and time series.
definitions.research: Liquid time-constant networks modelled by ODEs whose dynamics vary with input.

terms.analogy: Water reshaping to fit its container.
terms.example: Liquid neural networks flew a drone with only a few neurons.

definitions.beginner: Letting easy words skip some layers so the model spends effort only where needed.
definitions.builder: A router picks which tokens get processed at each layer; others skip via the residual path, saving compute.
definitions.research: Per-layer top-k token routing for dynamic compute allocation under a fixed budget.

terms.analogy: Express checkout for simple items.
terms.example: Mixture of depths cut FLOPs by half with no loss.

definitions.beginner: Letting each word look at only some others, so very long texts are cheaper to process.
definitions.builder: Local windows, strided or learned patterns replace full attention to cut quadratic cost on long contexts.
definitions.research: Attention restricted to a sparse pattern of pairs, reducing O(n²) to near-linear complexity.

terms.analogy: Reading only the paragraphs nearby plus the headlines.
terms.example: Sparse attention made 1M-token context practical.

definitions.beginner: An image and video generator that uses a transformer as its engine.
definitions.builder: Replaces the U-Net in diffusion with a transformer over image patches; scales cleanly and powers top video models.
definitions.research: Latent diffusion with a transformer backbone over patchified latents, conditioned via adaptive layer norm.

terms.analogy: Swapping the sculptor's tools for a power tool.
terms.example: The video model is a diffusion transformer.

definitions.beginner: Diffusion models described as smooth flows over time instead of fixed steps.
definitions.builder: SDE/ODE framing that lets you pick step counts and fast solvers at sampling time.
definitions.research: Score-based generative modelling via forward SDEs with reverse-time SDE or probability-flow ODE sampling.

terms.analogy: A film instead of a flipbook.
terms.example: Continuous-time diffusion allows 4-step sampling.

definitions.beginner: A model that squeezes images into a compact code and rebuilds them, used inside image generators.
definitions.builder: Encoder to latent distribution, decoder back; latent diffusion models run in a VAE's latent space.
definitions.research: Maximising the ELBO with a reparameterised Gaussian posterior and KL regulariser.

terms.analogy: Zipping and unzipping a picture.
terms.example: The VAE compresses each frame 8x before diffusion.

definitions.beginner: Two AIs competing, one creating fakes and one spotting them, until the fakes look real.
definitions.builder: Generator vs discriminator training; fast sampling but unstable, mostly superseded by diffusion.
definitions.research: Minimax game min_G max_D between generator and discriminator approximating the data distribution.

terms.analogy: A forger versus a detective.
terms.example: The first deepfakes were made with a GAN.

definitions.beginner: Image generators that create pictures piece by piece, like writing text one word at a time.
definitions.builder: Tokenise images and predict tokens sequentially; unifies image and text generation in one model.
definitions.research: Next-token (or next-scale) prediction over discrete visual tokens from a learned image tokenizer.

terms.analogy: Painting a mosaic tile by tile.
terms.example: The native image model is one of the autoregressive vision models.

definitions.beginner: A model that scores how plausible something is, low "energy" for likely, high for unlikely.
definitions.builder: Learns a scalar compatibility function; flexible but sampling and normalisation are expensive.
definitions.research: p(x) ∝ exp(−E(x)) with an intractable partition function, trained via contrastive or score methods.

terms.analogy: Marbles settling in valleys.
terms.example: An energy-based model ranks how realistic each scene is.

definitions.beginner: A network that models change continuously over time, using calculus.
definitions.builder: Layers become a learned differential equation solved by an ODE solver; memory-efficient, adaptive depth.
definitions.research: dh/dt = f(h, t; θ), integrated by numerical solvers with adjoint-based gradients.

terms.analogy: A smooth ramp instead of stairs.
terms.example: The neural ODE models patient vitals over time.

definitions.beginner: Microsoft's tech for training huge models by spreading their memory across many GPUs.
definitions.builder: ZeRO-1 shards optimiser state, ZeRO-2 adds gradients, ZeRO-3 adds parameters.
definitions.research: Zero Redundancy Optimizer stages removing replicated training state in data parallelism.

terms.analogy: Splitting a giant backpack's contents among hikers.
terms.example: DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 let us train on smaller GPUs.

definitions.beginner: NVIDIA's framework for training giant language models across thousands of GPUs.
definitions.builder: Reference implementation of tensor, pipeline and sequence parallelism for large-scale training.
definitions.research: Model-parallel transformer training combining intra- and inter-layer partitioning.

terms.analogy: Construction scaffolding for skyscraper-sized models.
terms.example: The lab trained its model with Megatron-LM.

definitions.beginner: A programming language that makes it easier to write fast code for AI chips.
definitions.builder: Python-like DSL from OpenAI for writing GPU kernels without raw CUDA; powers torch.compile kernels.
definitions.research: Block-level GPU programming model with automatic tiling and memory-hierarchy management.

terms.analogy: Power tools instead of hand tools for GPU code.
terms.example: We wrote a custom Triton kernel for our attention variant.

definitions.beginner: Hand-tuning the low-level code that runs on NVIDIA chips to squeeze out more speed.
definitions.builder: Fusing operations, tiling for shared memory and using tensor cores to approach peak FLOPs.
definitions.research: Optimising arithmetic intensity, memory coalescing and occupancy to move kernels toward the roofline.

terms.analogy: Tuning a race car's engine.
terms.example: CUDA kernel optimization doubled our training speed.

definitions.beginner: Newer, even faster versions of FlashAttention built for the latest GPUs.
definitions.builder: FA-2 improved parallelism and work partitioning; FA-3 uses Hopper async and FP8 for further speedups.
definitions.research: Warp-specialised, asynchronous pipelined attention kernels with low-precision support.

terms.analogy: Version 3 of a faster engine.
terms.example: FlashAttention-3 hits 75% of H100 peak.

definitions.beginner: Training a model while pretending it's already compressed, so it stays accurate when it actually is.
definitions.builder: Simulate low-precision rounding during training; better quality than post-training quantization at 4 bits and below.
definitions.research: Fake-quantisation in the forward pass with straight-through gradient estimators.

terms.analogy: Practising in the costume before the show.
terms.example: QAT kept the 4-bit model almost as good as full precision.

definitions.beginner: Compressing a finished model's numbers after training, without retraining it.
definitions.builder: Calibrate on a small dataset and round weights (GPTQ, AWQ); fast and cheap, some quality loss at low bits.
definitions.research: Quantisation solved as layer-wise reconstruction minimisation using calibration activations.

terms.analogy: Shrinking a photo after it's taken.
terms.example: PTQ got the model to 4 bits in an hour.

definitions.beginner: Running the "read the prompt" and "write the answer" phases on different machines to save cost.
definitions.builder: Phase-split serving placing prefill and decode on hardware suited to each.
definitions.research: Heterogeneous cluster scheduling exploiting prefill's compute-boundness and decode's memory-boundness.

terms.analogy: Separate kitchens for prep and plating.
terms.example: Splitwise cut serving costs by 20%.

definitions.beginner: Reusing work for repeated prompt beginnings across requests, inside the serving engine.
definitions.builder: Engine-level KV reuse (e.g. vLLM automatic prefix caching) for shared system prompts and documents.
definitions.research: Hash-indexed KV block sharing across sequences with common token prefixes.

terms.analogy: Pre-made pizza bases.
terms.example: Prefix caching made every request share the 10k-token system prompt.

definitions.beginner: Processing a long prompt in pieces so other users' answers don't stall.
definitions.builder: Split prefill into chunks interleaved with decode steps to smooth latency under load.
definitions.research: Co-scheduling prefill chunks with decode batches to balance utilisation and tail latency.

terms.analogy: Serving short orders while a big one cooks.
terms.example: Chunked prefill fixed our latency spikes.

definitions.beginner: Splitting AI serving into two specialised server pools, one reading prompts and one writing answers.
definitions.builder: Separate prefill and decode clusters, transferring KV caches between them; independent scaling and better SLOs.
definitions.research: Phase-disaggregated architecture with KV transfer, optimising goodput under TTFT/TPOT constraints.

terms.analogy: A restaurant with separate prep and cooking teams.
terms.example: Disaggregated prefill and decode improved our throughput 2x.

definitions.beginner: A preference-training method that only needs thumbs up or down, not side-by-side comparisons.
definitions.builder: Aligns with binary desirable/undesirable labels using a prospect-theory-inspired loss; easy to collect data for.
definitions.research: Human-aware loss modelling loss aversion from prospect theory over a reference point, without paired preferences.

terms.analogy: Learning from likes and dislikes.
terms.example: KTO used our product's thumbs-up data directly.

definitions.beginner: A method that teaches instructions and preferences in one training step.
definitions.builder: Combines SFT with an odds-ratio penalty on rejected answers, with no reference model needed.
definitions.research: Monolithic preference alignment adding a log-odds-ratio term to the NLL objective.

terms.analogy: Learning the rules and good taste in one class.
terms.example: ORPO saved us a whole training stage.

definitions.beginner: When one internal feature of a model means exactly one thing, versus many mixed meanings (polysemantic).
definitions.builder: Interpretability goal; sparse autoencoders turn polysemantic neurons into monosemantic features.
definitions.research: Features aligned to a single human-interpretable concept, contrasted with polysemantic neurons arising from superposition.

terms.analogy: One label per jar instead of a mixed bag.
terms.example: Monosemanticity research found a feature for "code bugs".

definitions.beginner: The challenge of keeping AI that's smarter than us aligned with human goals.
definitions.builder: Research on supervising superhuman systems, e.g. weak-to-strong generalisation and scalable oversight.
definitions.research: Aligning systems whose capabilities exceed evaluators', where direct human supervision is unreliable.

terms.analogy: Teaching someone who'll soon know more than you.
terms.example: The superalignment team studied weak-to-strong supervision.

definitions.beginner: Reading and editing an AI's internal "thoughts" to control traits like honesty.
definitions.builder: Find concept directions in activations (via contrast prompts) and add or subtract them to steer behaviour.
definitions.research: Top-down analysis of population-level representations enabling reading and control vectors.

terms.analogy: Tuning a mood dial inside the brain.
terms.example: Representation engineering made it more truthful.

definitions.beginner: Testing whether a model secretly knows something by training a tiny detector on its internals.
definitions.builder: Linear classifiers on hidden states reveal what information is encoded at each layer.
definitions.research: Supervised probes on activations measuring decodability, distinct from causal use.

terms.analogy: A stethoscope for neural networks.
terms.example: Feature probing showed it tracks the chessboard internally.

definitions.beginner: Attention parts that spot repeated patterns and predict what came next last time.
definitions.builder: Two-head circuits completing [A][B]…[A]→[B]; believed to drive much of in-context learning.
definitions.research: Composition of a previous-token head and a copying head, forming during a phase change in training.

terms.analogy: Remembering how the rhyme went last verse.
terms.example: Induction heads appear suddenly during training.

definitions.beginner: Tracing the exact path of computation inside a model for a specific behaviour.
definitions.builder: Identify the minimal subgraph of heads and features responsible, via activation patching and attribution.
definitions.research: Causal identification of computational subgraphs implementing algorithms within trained networks.

terms.analogy: Tracing wires in a circuit board.
terms.example: Circuit analysis showed how it adds two-digit numbers.

definitions.beginner: Secretly planting a hidden trigger in an AI during training so it misbehaves on cue.
definitions.builder: Poisoned training data teaches trigger-conditional behaviour that survives normal evals.
definitions.research: Data or weight poisoning inducing targeted behaviour on trigger inputs while preserving clean performance.

terms.analogy: A sleeper agent with a code word.
terms.example: The backdoor attack activated when a certain year appeared.

definitions.beginner: Corrupting an AI by slipping bad data into what it learns from.
definitions.builder: Few poisoned documents in web-scale data can implant behaviours; vet sources and monitor for triggers.
definitions.research: Adversarial manipulation of training data or updates to degrade or control a learned model.

terms.analogy: Spiking the well.
terms.example: Just 250 documents were enough for model poisoning.

definitions.beginner: Figuring out whether a specific piece of data was used to train an AI.
definitions.builder: Privacy attack exploiting lower loss on training examples; relevant to copyright and personal data claims.
definitions.research: Hypothesis testing on model outputs or losses to infer training-set inclusion.

terms.analogy: Checking if a student studied a particular page.
terms.example: A membership inference attack revealed the book was in the training set.

definitions.beginner: Malicious instructions hidden in webpages or files that an AI reads while doing a task.
definitions.builder: The attacker never talks to the model; payloads ride in tool results, emails or docs. Isolate privileges and confirm risky actions.
definitions.research: Injection via third-party content in the context, exploiting the absence of instruction/data separation.

terms.analogy: A booby-trapped letter in the mail pile.
terms.example: Indirect prompt injection in a calendar invite hijacked the agent.

definitions.beginner: Making an AI forget specific data or knowledge without retraining from scratch.
definitions.builder: Targeted fine-tuning or editing to remove personal data or hazardous knowledge; verify it's truly gone.
definitions.research: Approximating the model that would result from training without the forget set.

terms.analogy: Erasing one chapter from memory.
terms.example: Machine unlearning removed the leaked customer records.

definitions.beginner: Removing a specific idea, like an artist's style, from what a model can produce.
definitions.builder: Edit representations or weights so a concept is no longer usable or decodable.
definitions.research: Projecting out concept subspaces (e.g. LEACE) so no linear classifier can recover them.

terms.analogy: Blacking out a word in every book.
terms.example: Concept erasure stopped the model imitating that artist.

definitions.beginner: When a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure.
definitions.builder: Optimising a proxy (benchmark, reward model) eventually breaks its link to what you actually want.
definitions.research: Proxy–objective divergence under optimisation pressure; the theory behind reward hacking.

terms.analogy: Paying per line of code gets you long code.
terms.example: Goodhart's law is why the bot learned to flatter users.

definitions.beginner: Training a few invisible "prompt" vectors instead of the model to steer its behaviour.
definitions.builder: Learned continuous embeddings prepended to inputs (prompt / prefix tuning); tiny storage per task.
definitions.research: Optimising virtual token embeddings or per-layer prefix activations with frozen model weights.

terms.analogy: A secret handshake the model learns to respond to.
terms.example: Soft prompting gave us one tiny file per customer.

definitions.beginner: Small add-on layers plugged into a frozen model to teach it a new task.
definitions.builder: Bottleneck modules inserted between layers and trained alone; swappable per task.
definitions.research: Residual down-/up-projection blocks enabling parameter-efficient transfer.

terms.analogy: Plug-in modules for a modular synth.
terms.example: Each language gets its own adapters.

definitions.beginner: Representing a big table of numbers as the product of two thin ones, the trick behind LoRA.
definitions.builder: ΔW ≈ BA with rank r keeps updates tiny; r trades capacity for memory.
definitions.research: Low-rank factorisation exploiting the low intrinsic dimension of fine-tuning updates.

terms.analogy: Describing a picture with a few brush strokes.
terms.example: LoRA trains rank decomposition matrices instead of full weights.

definitions.beginner: The message or instructions you give an AI to get a response.
definitions.builder: The full input sent to the model: system prompt, conversation, documents and tool results. Its structure drives quality.
definitions.research: The conditioning context x on which the model samples p(y | x); small changes can shift outputs substantially.

terms.analogy: The brief you hand a very fast, very literal freelancer.
terms.example: A clearer prompt fixed the formatting problem.

definitions.beginner: Hidden instructions an app gives the AI before you start chatting, setting its role and rules.
definitions.builder: Operator-level instructions that persist across the conversation; where you put persona, policies, tools guidance and format.
definitions.research: A privileged context segment that models are trained to weight above user turns in the instruction hierarchy.

terms.analogy: The job description the assistant read before you walked in.
terms.example: The system prompt tells the bot to answer only about our product.

definitions.beginner: The skill of wording instructions so an AI gives you better results.
definitions.builder: Iteratively designing prompts (instructions, examples, structure) and testing them against evals instead of vibes.
definitions.research: Search over the discrete input space to elicit desired behaviour without updating parameters.

terms.analogy: Learning how to ask a genius coworker for help.
terms.example: A day of prompt engineering beat a week of fine-tuning.

definitions.beginner: Carefully choosing everything an AI gets to see, like documents, memory and tools, not just the question.
definitions.builder: Designing what fills the context window each turn (retrieved docs, tool results, memory, compaction) to maximise signal per token.
definitions.research: Optimising the information state presented to a model across steps of an agentic loop under a finite token budget.

terms.analogy: Packing a suitcase: what you bring matters more than how you ask.
terms.example: Context engineering made the agent stop forgetting the user's goal.

definitions.beginner: Showing an AI a few examples of what you want before asking it to do the real thing.
definitions.builder: Including input→output examples in the prompt to pin down format and style without any training.
definitions.research: In-context learning from k demonstrations; the model infers the task from examples at inference time.

terms.analogy: Showing a new hire three finished reports before they write the fourth.
terms.example: Few-shot prompting with three examples fixed the tone.

definitions.beginner: When an AI picks up a new task just from instructions or examples in the conversation, with no retraining.
definitions.builder: Task adaptation purely through the prompt; why demos and docs in context change behaviour instantly.
definitions.research: Emergent meta-learning in which transformers implement learning-like updates within the forward pass over context.

terms.analogy: Learning a board game by reading the rules on the box.
terms.example: In-context learning let it follow our made-up file format.

definitions.beginner: Getting an AI to work through a problem step by step before answering, which makes it more accurate.
definitions.builder: Intermediate reasoning tokens before the answer; now built into reasoning models via "thinking" rather than prompt tricks.
definitions.research: Generating latent reasoning traces that decompose computation across tokens, increasing effective serial compute.

terms.analogy: Showing your working in a maths exam.
terms.example: Chain-of-thought fixed most of its arithmetic mistakes.

definitions.beginner: A setting that controls how random or creative an AI's answers are.
definitions.builder: Sampling parameter scaling logits; low for deterministic extraction, higher for brainstorming. Some newer models fix it.
definitions.research: The divisor T in softmax(z/T); T→0 approaches greedy decoding, larger T flattens the distribution.

terms.analogy: A spice dial from "always the same" to "surprise me".
terms.example: Set temperature to zero for the data extraction step.

definitions.beginner: How a model picks each next word from its list of likely options.
definitions.builder: Decoding strategy (temperature, top-p, top-k) that turns next-token probabilities into actual text.
definitions.research: Drawing tokens from the model's predictive distribution, possibly truncated (nucleus) or reshaped, at each autoregressive step.

terms.analogy: Drawing from a bag where likelier words have more marbles.
terms.example: Nucleus sampling made the stories less repetitive.

definitions.beginner: Making an AI answer in a fixed format, like a form with set fields, so software can read it.
definitions.builder: Constraining responses to a JSON schema so outputs parse every time; no regex scraping of prose.
definitions.research: Constrained decoding that masks tokens violating a grammar, guaranteeing outputs lie in a formal language.

terms.analogy: Handing someone a form instead of a blank page.
terms.example: Structured output gives us valid JSON on every call.

definitions.beginner: When an AI states something false with total confidence, like a made-up fact or fake source.
definitions.builder: Fluent but unfounded output; reduce with grounding (RAG, citations), tool use, and evals that check factuality.
definitions.research: Generation unsupported by training data or provided context, arising from likelihood-driven decoding beyond calibrated knowledge.

terms.analogy: A confident dinner guest who never says "I don't know".
terms.example: The lawyer was fined after a hallucination produced fake cases.

definitions.beginner: Making an AI base its answers on real, provided sources instead of its memory.
definitions.builder: Tying outputs to supplied documents or tool results, ideally with citations, to cut hallucinations.
definitions.research: Conditioning generation on verifiable external evidence and attributing claims to it.

terms.analogy: Show me where it says that.
terms.example: Grounding every answer in our docs made support replies trustworthy.

definitions.beginner: Links or quotes showing exactly where an AI got its information.
definitions.builder: Model-emitted references to specific passages in provided sources, which users and evals can verify.
definitions.research: Attribution of generated spans to source segments, enabling precision/recall evaluation of support.

terms.analogy: Footnotes for chatbots.
terms.example: Turn on citations so reviewers can check every claim.

definitions.beginner: Making sure AI systems actually do what people intend and stay helpful, honest and harmless.
definitions.builder: Training and evaluation work (RLHF, constitutions, red teaming) that shapes model behaviour toward intended values.
definitions.research: The problem of specifying and robustly instilling objectives so capable systems pursue intended goals, even out of distribution.

terms.analogy: Making sure the genie grants the wish you meant, not the one you said.
terms.example: The lab doubled its alignment team.

definitions.beginner: Safety limits that stop an AI from producing harmful or off-topic responses.
definitions.builder: Input/output filters, classifiers and policy checks wrapped around a model to block unsafe or out-of-scope content.
definitions.research: External or trained-in constraints on a policy's action space, evaluated for robustness under adversarial inputs.

terms.analogy: The barriers on a mountain road.
terms.example: Guardrails stop the bank's bot from giving tax advice.

definitions.beginner: A trick prompt that gets an AI to ignore its safety rules.
definitions.builder: Adversarial input (role-play, encodings, many-shot) that bypasses a model's refusal training.
definitions.research: An input distribution shift that elicits policy-violating behaviour, exposing gaps between training and deployment.

terms.analogy: Talking your way past a bouncer.
terms.example: Jailbreaking worked by asking it to write "a movie script".

definitions.beginner: Hidden instructions in a webpage or document that trick an AI into doing something its user didn't ask for.
definitions.builder: Untrusted content (emails, pages, tool output) carrying instructions the model may follow; the top security risk for agents.
definitions.research: Confusion of data and instruction channels in LLMs, analogous to SQL injection, without a clean architectural separation.

terms.analogy: A note slipped into a package that says "the courier should give me your keys".
terms.example: A prompt injection in an email told the agent to forward the inbox.

definitions.beginner: Hiring people to attack an AI on purpose to find its dangerous weaknesses before release.
definitions.builder: Structured adversarial testing, human and automated, for harmful capabilities, jailbreaks and misuse.
definitions.research: Adversarial evaluation searching for failure modes beyond static benchmarks, increasingly automated with attacker models.

terms.analogy: Paying burglars to test your locks.
terms.example: Red teaming found the model could explain dangerous chemistry.

definitions.beginner: Training an AI using people's ratings of its answers, so it learns what humans prefer.
definitions.builder: Collect human preference comparisons, train a reward model, then optimise the LLM against it (e.g. PPO) with a KL leash.
definitions.research: Policy optimisation against a learned reward r(x,y) fit to pairwise preferences, regularised by KL to a reference policy.

terms.analogy: A chef improving from diners' thumbs up and down.
terms.example: RLHF turned the raw model into a polite assistant.
terms.origin: Christiano et al., 2017; scaled in InstructGPT, 2022.

definitions.beginner: Training an AI to follow a written set of principles, using AI feedback instead of only human ratings.
definitions.builder: Self-critique and AI-generated preference labels guided by an explicit constitution; scales harmlessness training.
definitions.research: RLAIF where a model judges outputs against natural-language principles to produce preference data, reducing human labelling.

terms.analogy: Giving a student a code of conduct and letting them grade their own essays against it.
terms.example: Constitutional AI lets the team change behaviour by editing principles.

definitions.beginner: When an AI finds a sneaky shortcut to score well on its training goal without doing the real task.
definitions.builder: Policies exploiting flaws in the reward signal, like editing tests so they pass. Watch for it in RL fine-tunes and agent evals.
definitions.research: Optimisation pressure exploiting misspecification between proxy reward and true objective (Goodhart's law).

terms.analogy: A student who learns the grader only checks word count.
terms.example: Reward hacking showed up when the agent deleted failing tests.

definitions.beginner: A helper AI trained to score answers the way humans would, used to train the main AI.
definitions.builder: A model mapping (prompt, response) to a scalar preference score; the optimisation target in RLHF.
definitions.research: A learned r_φ(x, y) fit with a Bradley–Terry loss on comparisons; its errors are what policies learn to exploit.

terms.analogy: A practice judge standing in for the real panel.
terms.example: The reward model preferred longer answers, so the bot got wordy.

definitions.beginner: A simpler way to train AI on human preferences, skipping the separate scoring model.
definitions.builder: Fine-tunes directly on chosen/rejected pairs with a classification-style loss; cheaper and more stable than PPO-based RLHF.
definitions.research: Closed-form reparameterisation of the KL-regularised RLHF objective as a logistic loss on policy log-ratios.

terms.analogy: Learning from "this one, not that one" without hiring a judge.
terms.example: DPO got us most of the RLHF gains in a day.

definitions.beginner: When an AI flatters you or agrees with you even when you're wrong.
definitions.builder: Preference-trained models over-agreeing with users; test for it and penalise it in training and evals.
definitions.research: Reward-model bias toward user-confirming responses that RL then amplifies; a canonical specification-gaming case.

terms.analogy: A yes-man employee.
terms.example: The sycophancy got so bad it praised obviously broken code.

definitions.beginner: A hypothetical AI that can do most thinking tasks as well as a human can.
definitions.builder: A loosely defined milestone; labs and contracts define it differently, from "most economically valuable work" to benchmarks.
definitions.research: Broadly capable systems matching or exceeding humans across cognitive tasks; definitions and timelines remain contested.

terms.analogy: A worker who can learn any job, not just one.
terms.example: Every CEO now has an AGI timeline.

definitions.beginner: A hypothetical AI far smarter than the best humans at almost everything.
definitions.builder: The step beyond AGI; central to frontier safety debates and lab mission statements.
definitions.research: Systems vastly exceeding human cognitive performance across domains, raising control and alignment problems.

terms.analogy: Not a smarter student, the whole university at once.
terms.example: The new lab says its only product will be ASI.

definitions.beginner: A fake but realistic video, image or voice of a real person, made with AI.
definitions.builder: Synthetic media impersonating real people; countered with provenance (C2PA), watermarking and detection.
definitions.research: Generative manipulation of identity attributes in media, an arms race between synthesis fidelity and forensic detection.

terms.analogy: Digital puppetry with someone's face.
terms.example: A deepfake of the CEO's voice approved the wire transfer.

definitions.beginner: Hiding an invisible signal in AI-made content so it can later be identified as AI-generated.
definitions.builder: Statistical or metadata marks (e.g. SynthID, C2PA) on outputs; robust for images, weaker for short or edited text.
definitions.research: Biasing sampling toward a keyed token subset to enable hypothesis tests for machine origin, trading off quality and robustness.

terms.analogy: An invisible signature in the paper.
terms.example: The EU wants watermarking on generated images.

definitions.beginner: When an AI treats some groups unfairly because of patterns in the data it learned from.
definitions.builder: Systematic skew in outputs across groups; audit with disaggregated evals, mitigate in data and post-training.
definitions.research: Statistical disparities in model behaviour across protected attributes, measured via fairness metrics that can conflict.

terms.analogy: A mirror that's slightly warped by whoever built it.
terms.example: Model bias showed up as a penalty for career gaps.

definitions.beginner: AI getting worse when it's trained mostly on content made by other AIs.
definitions.builder: Degradation from recursive training on synthetic data; avoid with fresh human data and careful filtering.
definitions.research: Progressive loss of distribution tails when models are trained on samples from previous generations' outputs.

terms.analogy: A photocopy of a photocopy of a photocopy.
terms.example: Researchers warn of model collapse as the web fills with AI text.

definitions.beginner: Europe's law that sets rules for AI based on how risky each use is.
definitions.builder: Risk-tiered regulation, with bans, high-risk obligations, transparency duties and GPAI model rules phasing in from 2025.
definitions.research: The first horizontal AI regulation, layering product-safety conformity assessment with systemic-risk duties for frontier models.

terms.analogy: Food safety rules, but for algorithms.
terms.example: The EU AI Act requires labelling deepfakes.

definitions.beginner: AI used in areas like hiring, credit or healthcare, where mistakes can seriously hurt people, so it faces stricter rules.
definitions.builder: A regulatory category requiring risk management, data governance, logging, human oversight and conformity checks.
definitions.research: Annex-listed use cases under the EU AI Act subject to ex-ante obligations proportional to potential harm.

terms.analogy: Like the extra inspections a passenger plane gets versus a kite.
terms.example: Our CV-screening tool counts as high-risk AI.

definitions.beginner: The legal name in Europe for big AI models that can be used for many different things.
definitions.builder: EU category for foundation models with transparency and copyright duties, plus extra obligations for "systemic risk" models.
definitions.research: Models displaying significant generality; systemic-risk presumption tied to training compute thresholds.

terms.analogy: A Swiss Army knife, regulated differently from a single blade.
terms.example: GPAI providers must publish a training data summary.

definitions.beginner: Controlling who gets powerful AI chips and how they're used, as a way to manage AI risks.
definitions.builder: Policy levers on chips and data centres (export controls, reporting thresholds, know-your-customer for cloud).
definitions.research: Governance via the physical, quantifiable, concentrated compute supply chain as a verifiable chokepoint.

terms.analogy: Regulating the factories that make engines, not every car.
terms.example: Export controls are compute governance in action.

definitions.beginner: Government rules that stop advanced AI chips from being sold to certain countries.
definitions.builder: US restrictions on advanced GPUs and chipmaking tools to specific destinations, shaping where frontier AI gets built.
definitions.research: Strategic trade policy targeting semiconductor chokepoints to slow rival frontier capabilities.

terms.analogy: Not selling engines to a rival racing team.
terms.example: Export controls made top GPUs hard to buy in some markets.

definitions.beginner: The most advanced AI models at any given time, at the edge of what's possible.
definitions.builder: State-of-the-art models from leading labs, the focus of safety testing, regulation and enterprise deals.
definitions.research: Models at or beyond the capability frontier, whose novel risks motivate pre-deployment evaluation regimes.

terms.analogy: The newest jets, not the trusty old planes.
terms.example: Only a few labs can afford to train a frontier model.

definitions.beginner: A lab's public promise to add stronger safety measures as its AI gets more capable.
definitions.builder: Capability thresholds tied to required safeguards, e.g. Anthropic's ASL levels; testing gates each release.
definitions.research: If-then commitments linking evaluated dangerous-capability thresholds to security and deployment safeguards.

terms.analogy: Safety rules that tighten as the lab handles more dangerous materials.
terms.example: Their responsible scaling policy triggered stricter security.

definitions.beginner: The legal question of whether training AI on copyrighted books, art and news is allowed without permission.
definitions.builder: US doctrine at the centre of AI training lawsuits; outcomes shape licensing deals and dataset choices.
definitions.research: A four-factor test (purpose, nature, amount, market effect) applied to the novel case of model training.

terms.analogy: Is reading every book in the library to learn to write "copying"?
terms.example: The court ruled on fair use for training data.

definitions.beginner: An app that is mostly a nice interface on top of someone else's AI model.
definitions.builder: A product whose core value is UX and workflow around a third-party API; moats come from data, distribution and integration.
definitions.research: Thin-layer applications exposed to platform risk when the underlying model provider expands downstream.

terms.analogy: A nice storefront selling someone else's bread.
terms.example: Investors worry it's just an AI wrapper.

definitions.beginner: Something that makes a company hard to copy or compete with.
definitions.builder: Durable advantages like proprietary data, distribution, workflow lock-in or cost, rarely the model alone.
definitions.research: Sustainable competitive advantage; in AI, contested as frontier capabilities diffuse quickly.

terms.analogy: The water around a castle.
terms.example: The team's moat is their exclusive medical data.

definitions.beginner: How AI APIs charge, a tiny fee for every chunk of text going in and coming out.
definitions.builder: Separate input and output rates per million tokens; output costs more. Caching and batching cut the bill.
definitions.research: Usage-based pricing reflecting prefill vs decode compute asymmetry and memory occupancy.

terms.analogy: A taxi meter that runs on words.
terms.example: The price per token fell 90% in a year.

definitions.beginner: One of the giant cloud companies, like Amazon, Microsoft and Google, that run huge data centres.
definitions.builder: Cloud providers selling GPU capacity and hosting models; also major investors in AI labs.
definitions.research: Firms operating global-scale infrastructure whose capex now dominates AI compute supply.

terms.analogy: The power companies of computing.
terms.example: Every hyperscaler raised its AI spending again.

definitions.beginner: The huge amounts companies spend building data centres and buying chips for AI.
definitions.builder: Capital expenditure on AI infrastructure; markets watch it as a bet on future AI revenue.
definitions.research: Front-loaded fixed investment whose return depends on inference demand growth and hardware depreciation.

terms.analogy: Building the railways before the trains are full.
terms.example: Big Tech's AI capex now tops hundreds of billions a year.

definitions.beginner: Low-quality, mass-produced AI content flooding the internet.
definitions.builder: Unreviewed generated text, images or video produced for clicks; a quality and trust problem for platforms.
definitions.research: Low-effort synthetic media whose prevalence threatens information ecosystems and future training corpora.

terms.analogy: Spam's lazy cousin.
terms.example: My feed is full of AI slop.

definitions.beginner: A critic's term for AI that repeats patterns of language without truly understanding it.
definitions.builder: A framing from the 2021 paper on risks of large LMs; still a shorthand in debates about understanding.
definitions.research: The claim that LMs stitch together linguistic forms by probability without reference to meaning.

terms.analogy: A parrot that can recite poetry.
terms.example: Critics called the chatbot a stochastic parrot.

definitions.beginner: A period when hype fades and money for AI research dries up.
definitions.builder: Historical funding crashes (1970s, late 1980s) after over-promising; invoked whenever a bubble is suspected.
definitions.research: Cycles of inflated expectation and retrenchment in AI funding and institutional support.

terms.analogy: The hangover after the party.
terms.example: Sceptics predict another AI winter.

definitions.beginner: The worry that AI company values and spending have grown faster than real profits.
definitions.builder: The debate over whether infrastructure spend and valuations outrun revenue, akin to the dot-com era.
definitions.research: Asset prices disconnected from discounted expected cash flows under speculative expectations.

terms.analogy: Paying mansion prices for a house still being built.
terms.example: Analysts argue about whether there's an AI bubble.

definitions.beginner: Slang for someone's estimated probability that AI leads to catastrophe.
definitions.builder: Half-serious shorthand in AI safety circles; useful as a conversation starter, not as data.
definitions.research: A subjective credence in existential catastrophe from AI, widely varying across experts.

terms.analogy: A weather forecast for the end of the world.
terms.example: Over dinner everyone shared their p(doom).

definitions.beginner: An online movement arguing AI progress should go as fast as possible.
definitions.builder: Pro-speed tech subculture contrasted with safety-focused "decels"; mostly shows up in discourse, not engineering.
definitions.research: Techno-optimist ideology favouring unrestricted capability growth, opposed to precautionary governance.

terms.analogy: Foot flat on the gas pedal.
terms.example: His bio just says e/acc.

definitions.beginner: Built around AI from day one rather than adding it later.
definitions.builder: Products and teams designed so models do core work; workflows, UI and pricing assume AI in the loop.
definitions.research: Organisational and product designs premised on model capabilities as a primary production input.

terms.analogy: Born digital versus scanned in.
terms.example: They're an AI-native law firm.

definitions.beginner: Using machines or software to do tasks people used to do by hand.
definitions.builder: With LLMs, automation reaches language-heavy work (support, drafting, coding) that rules-based systems couldn't handle.
definitions.research: Substitution of capital for labour in tasks; LLMs shift exposure toward cognitive, non-routine work.

terms.analogy: The dishwasher, but for paperwork.
terms.example: Automation handled 60% of support tickets.

definitions.beginner: Using AI to help people do their work better, rather than replacing them.
definitions.builder: AI as collaborator (drafts, suggestions, reviews) with humans deciding; often the faster path to adoption.
definitions.research: Complementarity between human and machine inputs, raising labour productivity without displacement.

terms.analogy: Power steering, not a self-driving car.
terms.example: The team chose augmentation over full automation.

definitions.beginner: A document describing what an AI model is for, how it was tested and its known limits.
definitions.builder: Release documentation covering intended use, evals, safety results and limitations; increasingly expected by regulators.
definitions.research: Standardised reporting of model provenance and disaggregated performance, proposed by Mitchell et al., 2019.

terms.analogy: The nutrition label on the box.
terms.example: The model card lists its known weaknesses.
